[f. 49v] … but would to God that this were the only ground of his hope [Navarre’s hope of seeing Paris fall through the “practice of commerce”]; but there are so many others besides, such as […] the instruction I sent to Your Most Illustrious Lordship with my letter of the twenty-sixth of November, and I shall speak of it in its place. May God help us! [f. 50r] As for the passports and letters patent issued on that occasion, […] precisely what I foretold has happened: although those letters had been partly amended by this Council before being published, they had not been put in such a form that one of them, fallen into Navarre’s hands, would not irritate him. […] and he has had orders given to hold back all that can be, and to hang without appeal those who carry them, saying that he did not mean to give Mayenne the whip to whip him with. Cardinal de Gondi, besides what he writes to me, has written to the Provost of the Merchants — who, at my instance, was inviting him back for these Christmas feasts, but on condition of the oath, to calm the people — that he would not swear. So he has not come. Meanwhile the service of the church […]. [f. 50v] [The Dean has admitted to others what he denies to me: that he spoke to Navarre,] “the handsome, the […] and the most favoured of all”, of whom, in the letter that was not left with me, a eulogy of purity and innocence is made […] to St John the Baptist and St John the Evangelist. One of the good canons complaining of it, and coming to words with another over whether or not to adhere to the heretic, the latter let slip that he would kiss even the devil rather than consent to the heretic to save himself; and no demonstration has been made of it. So I wrote to Cardinal de Gondi to order things as best he thought [for the Te Deum for the election of Gregory XIV], and have brought back an answer […]. [f. 51r] [The preachers] are all the more stirred up; indeed, in the said letter great complaint is made [of this opposition]: that Senlis [Guillaume Rose] and his followers are these seditious men and the cause of the controversy. […] the concert [with Navarre] is about to vanish; [Madame de Guise showed me a letter] from La Châtre; [he] had left Orléans on the twenty-seventh of last month for the Berry; […] left for Nemours. The Jesuit Provincial, seeing little hope of bearing fruit here, [goes to meet Mayenne]. [f. 51v] I did not go with them, so as not to hasten the loss of this city, since by staying it falls to me to keep [it] to its duty, if nothing else. [Mayenne] has sent the Count of Brissac here to explore by various means the true state of Paris: […] most unhappy and [most perilous], exposed to sedition, to escalade or some other stratagem, or to the will to surrender to another prince; and if he does not relieve it, […] let the enemy in. […] He came back on the night of the fourth and carries a letter of mine […]. We ask for a thousand paid Spanish and Italian foot, victuals for three months for them, […] where we have within the provision of food […] and about a hundred [and fifty] horse, […] and to order the neighbouring garrisons to keep in touch with these. [f. 52r] […] the escalade of Saint-Denis […]: if it came into our power, we could [hold] the enemy until the arrival of the Duke of Parma. If Mayenne then relieves [Paris], I do not leave; if he does not, being able [to leave] with the Duchess of Guise, I shall have satisfied my conscience and the world. Cardinal de Gondi [seeks the way] to separate the princes of the blood and the Catholic nobility from Navarre; [I put the flea in his ear: by making] the separation [and throwing themselves] at the Pope’s feet, [they] would easily place themselves under his protection [to obey the one] whom an assembly […] of the Holy See [would make king]. [f. 52v] [It is time to raise] the siege […]. Brissac: if Mayenne is not prompt and diligent, [he may find himself with a fistful of flies]; between the princes, the Catholic nobility and Navarre; not only of this city but of all the other cities of the Union; […] the Catholic nobility, already ruined by the vain hopes and promises of that man [Navarre]; [the greatest of services will be that] the Pope [declare] incurring the censures all who follow Navarre, ecclesiastics or laymen, unless they […] and swear within a certain time, [f. 53r] according to the formula I sent to Your Most Illustrious Lordship or another suitable one; and this monitory or declaratory […] would come in time, accompanied by a good warning [to the princes] of the Union about the errors […] to the prejudice of the good progress of the cause; […] for otherwise, through the obstinacy of some, the blindness of others and private interests, everything is running to ruin, as Your Most Illustrious Lordship will see from the enclosed copies of writings fabricated and sent […] to Melun, sent back by a […] to the Provincial, and which I had sent to Mayenne, so that [Your Lordship] may judge in your prudence whether what they contain is seditious […] and of all too evident truth. [f. 53v] […] Corbeil, […] Lagny, Saint-Cloud; […] the tightening of commerce; […] neither eat nor drink […]. Four [plots] have been discovered: at Orléans, one at Nantes, the second; the third at Chalon in Burgundy […]; [they have] written to Mayenne [that], as he is not strong enough to defend them, they will provide for themselves; [they ask] the King of Spain to receive them into his particular protection; […] for the service and glory of God. [And of all these plots no punishment is seen through the diligence] of Mayenne, [except that] of Orléans. [f. 54r] [As for that of] Chalon, [said to have been made with the participation] of the castellan of that citadel, [perhaps nothing more will come of it]; […] in the arsenal. [We wait to see what comes of the negotiation of] Brissac. […] of importance. [Impertinent resolutions are feared, born] from this third […] of the Council […] of President Le Maistre […]: [the first] cannot speak or discern; [the second …] married his niece […]; [the third is the soul] of Cardinal de Gondi; [the fourth is] the precipice. [The two are closely bound] with the deliberations […] the votes. […] in council; […] to Mayenne. [The most ridiculous battle in the world:] the City orders, the […] Parlement prevents, the […] Council opposes; [everything is done and undone,] one against the other, the deliberations […]. [f. 54v] [Mayenne, moreover, is so inconstant that he wants and does not want the same thing at the same moment.] Between the Parlement and the Sixteen, between the magistrate and those of the police, among the members of the Parlement themselves, one against the other, and with little obedience, all [turn against] this weak head; […] the author of the second [writing]; [and as this] head [speaks different languages according to the men] who surround him […]: thus, when the head aches, the other limbs languish (“dum caput dolet, cetera membra languent”). [But no more of this for now: the writing will treat more fully] of the defects of the Union. [Meanwhile, may Your Most Illustrious Lordship think of the remedy, which] would be to have the Pope asked to take under the protection, government and tutelage of the Holy See this city with the whole Île-de-France, [until an Assembly of the Estates and the canonical election of a Catholic and Most Christian King], when opportune, [to bring some order] to these confusions, and to turn the war away from these parts by the authority of His Holiness, excommunicating all [who molest the Catholics] […] the State, with which they colour … [the copy stops here].

Reading notes and historical notes

  1. Context. At the end of November 1590 Paris has just been relieved by Alessandro Farnese; the League holds the city, Henry of Navarre the countryside. The clear passage before the cipher speaks of a bishop held prisoner, against whom “probationes probatas” are claimed, of the “sacrilege” that causes a great stir, and of requests for his “rilassatione”. The cipher keeps for the cardinal Sega’s own judgement: the bishop leans to the “opposite party” (Navarre’s) out of religious lukewarmness rather than calculation, and the nuncio will temporise to make the parties talk. On f. 17v, in clear, he wishes His Holiness to unmask (“smarcischi”) those who “seguitano il partito contrario”, with the declaratory: the same phrase as in the cipher.
  2. Probable words. {qulche}: certain digits qu-l-c-h-e, the “a” is missing (clerk’s omission), “ho qualche informatione”; della and natura (first probable) were confirmed by a blind re-reading of the sign shapes (plate of 29 Oct 2026: code letter x of della; 6 with ² of natura) and now count as certain; {vescovo}: the 6 with ² (u) looks like an 8, as in “natura” and “esecutione” where the u is certain; {contrario}: one 2 of 22 (c) unclear, the phrase recurs in clear on f. 17v; quello (first probable): sign ρ = code letter p, “vomitar tuto quello che sano”; confirmed by a blind re-reading of the shapes (plate of 29 Oct 2026: same shape as the p of “per” in clear in the same hand), counted certain.
  3. Unresolved. ‹canonizatorio›: the digits are certain (22 42 31 32 31 28 62 2̈ | 37 32 35 28 32), the sense in the sentence is not established. ‹c›: 22 followed by a dotted 9 (null); “c’un giorno” is not assured.
  4. Sega’s other letters. For the letter of 9 January 1591, Francia 32 keeps the contemporary decipherment (DECODE R5613), agreeing with George Lasry’s reading of the BnF copy (fr. 3613). The letter of 2 July 1591 (DECODE R5618) uses another system: digits without signs, many 1s, 7s and 9s; under a criterion fixed before calculation, key no. 65 segments only 62.5% of the pairs (threshold 85%) and is rejected.
  5. Prior work. No edition of Sega’s 1590–1591 dispatches is known (the Acta Nuntiaturae Gallicae do not cover Sega; M. Penzi, 2017, is a study); Daniel Bourdeau’s catalogue had listed these letters (no. 881, entry since withdrawn).
  6. The letter of 16 January 1591. “Umena” (128) is the Duke of Mayenne, head of the League. Probable words: {provinciale} (a doubtful isolated 2 before the 6 topped with ²; the clear text above mentions the Capuchin Fathers), {intercesione} (open 3 close to 7), {questa} {causa} (Δ, Meister’s symbol for questi, followed by “a”, then “ccausa”: the cipher clerk’s spelling), {rapresentata} (open 3 close to 9), {così} (one 3 too many before the null 9̈). Hypothesis: the “pomo” awaited “tanti et tanti anni” may be the red hat; Sega was created cardinal by Innocent IX in December 1591. Transcription frozen (SHA-256) before decoding, made with the key in mind as for f. 17.
  7. The whole of letter R5615 — partial reading. Method: Meister’s key no. 65 (1906), applied without retouching by a private tool; the key was validated on a held-out piece, the contemporary decipherment R5621 f. 230 (“che va inserto nella lettera di Mons. Sega delli 21 di Decembre 1590”): 0.934 in characters, 0.862 in words. The cipher was transcribed in 88 blocks, each frozen (SHA-256 fingerprint) before decoding; the transcription was made with the key in mind (declared bias: the known key steers the splitting of pairs). Values given by Meister’s printed key but absent from the tool (ω = in, ⊥ = più, ⧺ = ma, o– = già, ∞ = della, barred 4 = gli, ‖_ = con, Δ + vowel = quest-) count at best as probable; re-readings made after decoding (pairs split at line ends, stray isolated digits, “tailed 3” read as 3) are declared and count at best as probable. Brice’s blind re-reading (sign shapes, no gloss) is applied: {preuosto} and {letera} become certain; the blotted sign of the word read {bono} remains illegible (unresolved). Limits: a long-s sign with a crook (ʃ, six times, always before a noun: presumably “il”) is not in the printed key and stays unresolved; δ at the head of a clause reads 6 = u by the key while the sense often calls for che (left unresolved); the denser pages ff. 51v–54r have many misaligned pairs. Restored: [di] (f. 50r), determina[t]ioni (f. 54r), ce[t]era (f. 54v). Names: 128 Umena = Mayenne, 129 = Navarre, 229 = Cardinal de Gondi, 145 = the Union, 144 = France, 428 = His Holiness; “Sedeci” = the Sixteen; “le Mastre” = Jean Le Maistre, president in the League Parlement; “Sciatre” = La Châtre; “Brisac” = Brissac; “Sanclu” = Saint-Cloud. Content (summary). League Paris, blockaded by Henry of Navarre, in early January 1591: the commerce negotiation, passports, Cardinal de Gondi’s refusal to take the oath of the Union, canons tempted to rally, preachers against “Senlis”; the legate stays in the city to hold it; Brissac’s mission for Mayenne; a request for a thousand Spanish and Italian foot and for victuals; hopes of taking Saint-Denis by escalade while waiting for the Duke of Parma; a plan to detach the princes of the blood and the Catholic nobility from Navarre; a monitory against Navarre’s followers; plots discovered at Orléans, Nantes and Chalon; a divided Union government (City, Parlement, Council) and a “weak head” (Mayenne); the proposed remedy: to place Paris and the Île-de-France under the protection of the Holy See until the Estates and the canonical election of a Catholic king.

Method, validation and credits

Method (protocol written and hashed before calculation): (1) key K65 taken unchanged from Meister; (2) held-out validation on Sega’s letter of 21 December 1590, whose contemporary decipherment Francia 32 keeps (f. 230, “decifrato 26 di Marzo 1591”, DECODE R5621), transcribed and frozen before the corresponding cipher (ff. 228v, 231) was deciphered: the key applied unchanged agrees on 93.4% of characters (268/287) and 86.2% of words (56/65), against at most 55.1% and 49.2% for 200 controls with permuted key (word codes unchanged); 0.85 / 0.75 criterion met; (3) transcription of the f. 17r–v passage frozen (SHA-256) before decoding. Caveat: the transcriptions were made with the key in mind. Files in our research folder.

Credits. Key: A. Meister, Die Geheimschrift im Dienste der päpstlichen Kurie (1906), no. 65; its application to Sega’s letters: George Lasry (letter of 9 January 1591, BnF fr. 3613). Listing: Daniel Bourdeau’s catalogue, no. 881. Document: Archivio Apostolico Vaticano, Segr. Stato, Francia 32; images consulted on DECODE R5612 (and R5616, R5615, R5621, R5613, R5618), not reproduced. Transcription, decipherment, text, translation and notes: Brice Dudout, with Claude (Anthropic), October 2026.

The “Estat du Roy de Navarre”, c. 1583: the enciphered complaints of a Huguenot memoir

A memoir in French on “the state of the King of Navarre and of his party in France”, written in the first person by a man of the Reformed party (“our provinces”, “the letters have come into my hands”) and kept among the papers of an English secretary of state, slips some hundred lines of cipher into its plain text. These are the sensitive passages: the secret organisation of the churches, the reasons for keeping the surety towns, Monsieur’s dealings with the Prince of Parma, and reproaches to “the Queen”, who “has not spent a penny” on them since 1570. Daniel Bourdeau had recovered the alphabet; we re-read the signs on the image and read the text.

Date c. 1583 (hypothesis: “ce faict d’Anuers” = the “French Fury” at Antwerp, 17 January 1583; Monsieur, Duke of Anjou, alive and unmarried, so before June 1584)
Place France (King of Navarre’s party) → England (hypothesis: a paper meant for the court of Elizabeth I)
Author Anonymous Huguenot author, close to the King of Navarre
Recipient An unnamed foreign reader, probably English (the piece is filed among a secretary of state’s papers)
Source British Library, Harley MS 1582, fols. 263r–264v; images DECODE R8505 and DECODE R8010 (higher resolution), not reproduced here.
Cipher Homophonic substitution with about 50 graphic signs (Greek letters, hooks, barred omegas, Π, Ш…), dot groups = m, and about ten nomenclator numbers between dots (6, 21, 36, 51, 57, 72, 81, 99, 721), not read

Keywords ce faict d’Anuers · le prince de Parme · ele n’a pas despende un denier pour eu · se renforcer d’aliances

DECODE record R8010 ↗
DECODE record R8505 ↗
Bourdeau catalogue, no. 121 ↗

State of the reading. Partial reading, explained; unpublished to our knowledge. The key is Daniel Bourdeau’s, applied unchanged; his 2026 decoding was left as “decoded, not read” (about half the sentences clean). Published under Daniel Bourdeau’s rule: 95% of the words read in their sense. Here, for the cipher passages of fols. 264r and 264v: 666 words, 629 read (certain + probable, 94.4%), 635 (95.3%) with the restored words: 533 certain (80.0%), 96 probable (14.4%), 6 restored (0.9%) and 31 unresolved (4.7%). Code numbers are not counted. Fols. 263r–263v are not covered here. Without the restored words the 95% threshold is not reached (four words short); many probable words come from pairs of easily confused signs (see the notes).

Conventions: {x} = probable reading; [x] = letter restored from the sense; ‹x› = unresolved; [72] = code number not read; in grey, the plain text of the original (shortened “…”). Spelling of the cipher kept (Rhosne, deffiance, etecuté, despende); apostrophes added.

Established text (French)

Folio 264r

2.1–2.4 cependant ne laissent d’avoir un ordre et une forme de conduite, bien que plus secrete, et n’i a {petit} {coin} {ou} il n’i ait quelque {gentiliome} capable {et} {signalle}, auquel {s’adressent} les affaires, qui en un {besoing} seroit suiui {et} obei des autres.

2.5–2.7 ia {conseil} ‹e› establi ‹a› … les quels {raportent} ‹touui› au ‹lerpleo›

2.8–2.15 en cest affaire … les {causes} de {deffiance} durent encor, veu {que} {l’edict} n’est {etecuté} en un seul article, veu que de toutes les {contrauentions} on se plaint en uain, veu les {de[s]loiautes} qu’on uoit {tous} les {iours} pratiquer a {l’endroit} de ceus de la religion, veu aussi les {preparatifs} {et} ‹leuss› qui ia se {font} en Suisse et Alemagne, les munitions {qui} {s’amassent} a {Lion} pour couler {tout} a coup par le Rhosne, et les troupes qui s’envoient en Gascongne ‹luia›. Doncque les causes de defiance durent et multiplient ; la raison de {les} {retenir} {demeure} pareillement en son entier

2.16–2.25 de {diferer} la {rendition} des dites places, si on se boioit asseure d’une bonne armee de {reistres} qui peust {tenir} la campagne et {esloig[n]e[r]} la guerre {du} centre de nos {provinces} vers la {circonference} de la France … a {diferer} la remise {d’iceles} ; et quand nos ennemis … {s’il} ne {uoit} plus clair au secours de {dehors} {qu’il} n’a veu {iusques} a present, il se resoudra … puis {qu’il} ne la peut retenir par plus fortes {et} asseurees … {si} les moiens luy {sont} refuses par ceus pour la conservation desquele il ne {trauaille} guere a moings que pour la sienne, et ‹qua› en la {siene} ‹ie› {son[t]} guere a moins interesses {que} luy.

Folio 264v

3.1–3.2 … soin en leur {entretenant} e suscitant des ‹etdices› et ‹trauins› qui diuerrissent leur esprit et leurs moiens aleurs … comme le

3.4–3.5 … et espousera les {affections} e {factions} du {Pape}, qui doresenauant le {fera} son bras {droidt} e il {egecuteur} de ses plus ‹pernumieuq› {desseings}.

3.7–3.12 … cest de se rendre ou {chef} ou instrument principal de la ruine de ceus de la religion, come ainsi soit quil ne peut desguiser ce faict d’Anuers autrement … sans la victoire de Monsieur de ‹belueur› en l’aloit {traiter} auec le prince de Parme pour lui rendre les places qu’il {tenoit} ‹auoe› ‹sia› ‹tecee› {qu’il} lui ‹cissuada›

3.16–3.21 … ou sans doute le ‹roa› ‹adn› frere craindra quil ne releue contre lui {un} ‹parta› de malcontens … quelque desseing en Angleterre et Escosse … italien qui sert d’ingenieur a Lisbone, dont les letres me sont uenues es mains

3.22–3.24 … pour le reioindre auec [c]este maison ennemie de la chrestiente ‹eu› {particulierement} de l’estat d’Angleterre ; a quoi, ueu les pratiques ordinaires de ‹ceuo› de Guise en Escose, … doit remedier.

3.25–3.33 … {chef} de la guere contre ceus de la religion en le son frere a ‹deefietant› du roi son frere … quil … la charge d’une armee … a sa deuotion, ce qui lui a ‹aparende› que le roi lui permete … ‹scaiie› bien … le {s[e]ul} mariage d[e] … cest ‹tau› reste un prince qui … sortir de la une {armee} de reistres pour la ieter et espandre sur le pais de celui qui …

3.34–3.36 … tandis que le party de ceus de la religion demeurera ferme en [72] et ‹es› [99] les [81] [36] auront {peu} de moien de lui malfaire ; et pourtant ele a interest a ne les laisser perdre. … et {pour} les

3.37–3.41 … {quand} a la {France} … et qu’ele a la verite n’a traites ni selon sa qualite ni selon la leur, ele les a abandonnes en leur besoin, les a {laissee}, en tant qu’en ele a esté, et en risee et en {proie} a leurs ennemis, les a mesmes {traitee} {indignement} en leurs personnes et des {leurs} qui est gratuite e honorable enuers tous autres, et non de tele qualite qu’eus. Cela faut quy ne ‹suoset› {plus} atendre a son amitie, qu’ils ont tant {recherchee} en uain, et ne sauent s’il lui {font} plaisir de luy ofrir leur seruice.

3.42–3.46 On … la Roine quelle a faict merueille e quelquun … Mais elle se peut souuenir que depuis lan 70 ele n’a {pas} {despende} {un} denier pour eu ‹dencor› {que} Jamais Je n’en di tam d’affect … Et croy a quelle fin lan 79 moiennant certaines ‹baones› … Car quant aux deniers prestez lan 1576 c’est a Monseigneur qui les a … a ce respondre … {qui} {peut} estre {eussent} bien este {aussi} {utilement} {emploiee} {ailleurs}. Si est ce que {les} …

3.48–3.49 pour reuenir aux deux points proposez a {sauoir} les moiens que ‹lelent› tenir e ‹alonrs› se renforcer d’aliances, et pour {diuertir} les {efforts} de ses ennemis sans {beaucoup} {s’imcomoder}.

Translation

264r. … they nonetheless have an order and a form of conduct, though more secret: there is no corner so small that there is not some capable and notable gentleman, to whom business is addressed and who in need would be followed and obeyed by the others. … a council already set up … who report …

In this matter the causes of distrust still last: the edict is not carried out in a single article; of all the breaches one complains in vain; every day one sees disloyalty practised against those of the religion; preparations are already being made in Switzerland and Germany; munitions are being gathered at Lyon to come down the Rhône all at once; troops are being sent into Gascony. So the causes of distrust last and multiply, and the reason for keeping [the towns] remains whole:

to put off the surrender of the said towns, if one could be sure of a good army of reiters able to hold the field and to carry the war away from the centre of our provinces to the circumference of France … to put off handing them over; and when our enemies … if he sees no clearer about help from outside than he has so far, he will resolve … since he cannot keep it by stronger and surer [means] … if the means are refused him by those for whose preservation he works hardly less than for his own, and who are hardly less concerned in his than he is.

264v. … by keeping up and stirring up among them [troubles] that turn their minds and means elsewhere … and [Monsieur] will espouse the inclinations and factions of the Pope, who will henceforth make him his right arm and the executor of his most [pernicious] designs. … It is to make himself the head or the chief instrument of the ruin of those of the religion, since he cannot otherwise disguise the Antwerp affair … [without the victory] of Monsieur … they were going to negotiate it with the Prince of Parma, to hand back to him the towns he held …

… where no doubt the [king his] brother will fear that he may raise against him a party of malcontents … some design in England and Scotland … an Italian who serves as an engineer at Lisbon, whose letters have come into my hands … to join him to that house, the enemy of Christendom and particularly of the state of England; which, given the usual practices of those of Guise in Scotland, … must remedy.

… head of the war against those of the religion … of the King his brother … the command of an army devoted to him, which has [made him hope] that the King would allow it … the mere marriage of … remains a prince who … bring an army of reiters out of there to throw and spread it over the country of the one who …

… as long as the party of those of the religion stands firm, [codes 99, 81, 36] will have little means of harming him; and yet she has an interest in not letting them be lost.

As for France … in truth she has treated them neither according to her rank nor to theirs; she has abandoned them in their need, left them, as far as lay in her, to be mocked and preyed on by their enemies, has even treated them shamefully in their persons and those of their people — [which is free and honourable] towards all others, and not of such a quality as they. [So they can] no longer expect anything from her friendship, which they have sought so long in vain, and they do not know whether it pleases her that they offer her their service.

[They say the Queen has done wonders… But she may remember that since the year 1570] she has not spent a penny on them … in return for certain … [As for the money lent in 1576, it is for Monseigneur, who had it, to answer for it …] which might well have been as usefully employed elsewhere. Still, the …

[To return to the two points proposed:] namely the means that [the King of Navarre must] take to strengthen himself with alliances, and to divert the efforts of his enemies without putting himself to much inconvenience.

Reading notes and historical notes

  1. Date (hypothesis). “Ce faict d’Anuers” (264v) very probably means the “French Fury”, Francis of Anjou’s failed coup on Antwerp on 17 January 1583; the text also speaks of Monsieur as alive and unmarried (before June 1584), of Épernon and Joyeuse, and of an Italian engineer at Lisbon (after 1581). Hence c. 1583, rather than the 1580 of the catalogue title. The setting may be Ségur-Pardaillan’s missions to England and Germany (1583–1584); this is not verified.
  2. “The Queen”. The reproaches of 264v (“she has not spent a penny on them” since 1570; “money lent in 1576”) probably aim at Elizabeth I, whose 1576 loan paid for John Casimir’s army. That is precisely the part the author put in cipher. A reading hypothesis, not checked in the English papers.
  3. The code numbers (6, 21, 36, 51, 57, 72, 81, 99, 721) are not read. 81 = the King (Henry III), 21 = Monsieur, 51 = the King of Navarre have been suggested, but these values are not established.
  4. What the re-reading changed. The working transcription confused neighbouring signs: closed o and open cup (n / i), plain and barred loop (n / u), lunate ε and two-bowled ε (a / s), barred ε and delta (t / a), X and hourglass (l / p). It also filed several different signs under one name (a lying ⊣ = c, a ⅃ = c, a rounded U = h, a mere lead-in stroke). On 264v a line given to the foot of the page was in fact the rising end of the next line (“d’aliances”): it is counted once. An isolated dot attached to the ʃ (“qu’ele”, “esté”, “tenoit”, “traiter”) is read as a mark, not as m: “tenoit” and “traiter” count as probable; for “qu’ele” and “esté” the blind re-reading (next note) confirmed the mark.
  5. Targeted blind re-reading. Twelve doubtful signs of 264v were shown to a reader (Brice Dudout) with no letter or value: he chose the shape he saw among certain shapes taken elsewhere in the letter. The effect of each answer had been fixed and hashed (SHA-256) before the answers, then applied as it stood. Six words move from probable to certain (“qu’ele”, “tant”, “esté”, “ofrir”, “seruice”, “denier”); two stay probable but read “laissee” and “traitee” (the last sign is e, not s: an unusual agreement); “recherchee”, “font” and “despende” stay probable (no clear choice); the first sign of ‹cissuada› is confirmed as c. No word became unresolved.
  6. Still unresolved: 31 words, including whole stretches in 3.10–3.12 (after “de Monsieur de”), 3.29–3.30 and 3.43–3.44 (‹dencor›, ‹baones›). ‹cissuada› would read “dissuada” if its first sign were d; it is c in the key, and a restoration never overrides a certain sign.

Method, validation and credits

The key is Daniel Bourdeau’s (about 50 signs plus the dot groups), applied unchanged. Before reading with it, we tested it on two lines that nobody had yet transcribed: the end of fol. 264v, missing from the working transcription. We transcribed them from the image and froze the copy (SHA-256 hash) before any decipherment. The criterion was fixed in advance: at least 85% of the characters must form French words, and the key must beat 200 control keys with permuted letters. Result, in a single measurement: 0.886, against at best 0.737 for the controls. So it ranks 1st of 201. The difficult lines of fol. 264v were then re-transcribed sign by sign from the image, and the copy frozen before decipherment. This re-reading was not blind: the earlier decoding was known. Every doubtful sign was marked, and any word that depends on one counts as probable. The count follows Daniel Bourdeau’s rule.

Credits. Listing, alphabet and key: Daniel Bourdeau, catalogue no. 121 (folder harley1582r8505). Document: British Library, Harley MS 1582, fols. 263–264; images DECODE R8505 and DECODE R8010, not reproduced. Sign re-reading, transcription, validation, established text, translation and notes: Brice Dudout, with Claude (Anthropic), October 2026.

End of July 1662: “the Swedes are arming” — an enciphered letter in the Sanguszko archive

An unsigned Polish letter, dated in clear on the last day of July 1662, enciphered throughout with 23 composite sign groups. No contemporary decipherment, no key. We broke it from the ciphertext alone, checked it on the held-out reverse, and read it in full.

Date 31 July 1662 (“Ultima Julij A° 1662”, in clear at the head)
Place not stated; the writer is in a region “towards the sea” where the Elector of Brandenburg is expected (Prussia?)
Sender unknown (a few clear words at the end: “… MM Pan”, a form of address)
Recipient unknown (a lord, “MM Pan”)
Source Kraków, Archiwum Narodowe, Archiwum Sanguszków, teka 134/8; 2 pages; DECODE R7513
Cipher Simple substitution: each letter is written as a composite group of three or four strokes (digits, letters, squares, triangles: ☐78O = t, 15☐c = e, 50lF = i, 83yΔ = o…); 23 groups, no word division, punctuation kept; a cross over a marks ą

Key words Szwedzi armuią · woyne meditantur · z pod Lwowa … do Gd. anska · Curfirst … in Augusto

DECODE record R7513 ↗
Bourdeau catalogue, no. 443 ↗

Reading status. First published decipherment, to our knowledge. 320 groups, 71 words. Published under Daniel Bourdeau’s rule: 95% of words read as sense, counted on the enciphered part only. Here: 71 of 71 words read as sense (100%): 67 certain (94.4%), 3 probable (4.2%), 1 restored from the sense (1.4%), 0 unresolved. Reasons in the notes.

Conventions: {x} = probable reading; [x] = restored from the sense. The cipher’s spelling is kept (iusz, kozdemu, bydz, Hamburku); the cipher has no signs for ś, ż, ę, ł: they are not added to the established text but appear in the modern Polish reading.

Established text (Polish, cipher spelling)

Te nas wiesci dochodza z Rygiy y z Hamburku, ze sie Szwedzi armuią y iusz to trzeci raz zapowiedzie[i]li modlitwy y post. Co nieomylnie iest znakiem, ze woyne meditantur, y ze {kogs} zagabną.

Ia radze, zeby tey sciany ku morzu nie zostawowac ogoloconey, bo daleko z pod Lwowa bedzie do Gd. anska sie wracac.

Sam [… MM Pan] zdrowie swoie miey na pieczy y nie kozdem{u} duchowi wierz. Cur{f}irst pewnie tu ma bydz in Augusto.

Modern Polish reading

Te nas wieści dochodzą z Rygi i z Hamburga, że się Szwedzi zbroją i już to trzeci raz zapowiedzieli modlitwy i post. Co nieomylnie jest znakiem, że wojnę meditantur [rozważają], i że kogoś zagabną.

Ja radzę, żeby tej ściany ku morzu nie zostawiać ogołoconej, bo daleko z pod Lwowa będzie do Gdańska się wracać.

Sam [… MM Pan] zdrowie swoje miej na pieczy i nie każdemu duchowi wierz. Kurfirst pewnie tu ma być in Augusto [w sierpniu].

Translation

These are the news that reach us from Riga and from Hamburg: the Swedes are arming, and this is already the third time they have ordered prayers and a fast. That is the unfailing sign that they are contemplating war and will attack someone.

I advise that this side, towards the sea, should not be left bare: it would be a long way to come back from beneath Lwów to Gdańsk.

You yourself, [… my Lord,] take care of your health, and do not believe every spirit. The Elector will surely be here in August.

Reading notes and historical notes

  1. The moment. In 1662 Sweden held Riga and Livonia under the Peace of Oliva (1660). The writer reads the public prayers and fasts ordered in Sweden as the herald of a war. The Crown army was then in the south-east, around Lwów, where the confederation of unpaid soldiers (1661–1663) occupied the country: hence the advice not to strip “the side towards the sea” (Royal Prussia, Gdańsk). “Kurfirst” is the Elector of Brandenburg, Frederick William, duke in Prussia; he came to Königsberg in the autumn of 1662 to bring the Prussian estates to heel. Where the writer was is not stated: Prussia is a hypothesis.
  2. “Do not believe every spirit.” First Epistle of John 4:1, “nie każdemu duchowi wierzcie” in the Wujek Bible (1599): a warning against false rumours.
  3. Probable words and the restored word. {kogs}: letters certain; we take it as “kogoś” (someone), written short; a proper name is not excluded. kozdem{u} and Cur{f}irst: on the reverse, two groups occur only once and were not in the key drawn from the front: Ꝑt33, a variant of ϕt33 (u), and Mig4, f from the sense (Curfirst = Kurfürst). zapowiedzie[i]li: one group is partly covered by an ink blot; place and sense give i.
  4. Punctuation. Stops and commas are the cipher’s own; “Gd. anska” is written with a stop in the middle (“do Gdańska”). Between “Sam” and “zdrowie” the writer left a few words in clear (“… MM Pan”), not transcribed in full here (uncertain reading) and not counted.

Method, validation and credits

Method. Atlas of the 23 groups frozen before any computation; protocol written and hashed before computation; front (21 lines, 254 groups) for learning, reverse (6 lines, 66 groups) held out and never decoded before the key was frozen. Broken by simulated annealing on a Polish letter model (Latin, French, German and Italian score clearly lower); the Polish reads at once; two values corrected from the reading of the front only (g and k).

Validation. One measurement on the reverse: 97% of groups have a value; 86% of letters fall in words of the Polish lexicon (segmentation fixed in advance), against at most 58% for 200 permuted keys and at most 70% for 200 shuffled texts. The held-out reverse is short (66 groups): we say so.

Credits. Item listed by Daniel Bourdeau (catalogue, no. 443). Images: DECODE, R7513, reproduction from the Archiwum Narodowe w Krakowie, consulted for study and not reproduced here. Decipherment: Brice Dudout, with Claude (Anthropic), 29 October 2026.

Antonio Pérez to Don John of Austria: “not a single real”, Madrid, 19 August 1578

August 1578. Don John of Austria, half-brother of Philip II and governor of the Netherlands, is in the field against the States General and asking for money. Antonio Pérez, Secretary of State, answers him from Madrid in his own hand, after the arrival of Don John’s envoy, Don Alonso de Sotomayor. Four passages are in cipher. They say that the Council of Finance has “not a single real”, that providing what is needed is “impossible”, and that the asiento just made will not be followed by another. Don John died six weeks later, on 1 October; Pérez was arrested in July 1579 for the murder of Escobedo, Don John’s secretary.

Date 19 August 1578 (filing date “Ag.to 19. de 1578”); autograph
Place Madrid → the Netherlands
Sender Antonio Pérez, Secretary of State to Philip II
Recipient Don John of Austria, governor general of the Netherlands
Source Real Academia de la Historia (Madrid), Library, 2/Ms Caja 8 nº 4 (Fernández San Román collection), images 2–3.
Cipher numerical syllabary of the Spanish chancery of 1577, a variant of the table of the Genoa embassy: number = consonant (6 d, 7 c, 15 l, 16 m, 17 n, 20 p, 22 r, 23 s, 24 t…), mark after the number = vowel (+ a, . e, 6 i, hook o, ı u), single numbers 10 a, 4 e, 18 o, 1 u, superscripts ^ n, ¯ s, ˇ r, ′ l. In Pérez’s hand 8 is g (b in the Genoa table) and “8 with a small 2” is ble

Keywords por no aver un real · tengo por imposible · con protesto · consejo de hazienda

Images (RAH Biblioteca Digital) ↗
Validation pair: AGS Estado 1410,65–66 (PARES) ↗

State of the reading. First published decipherment, to our knowledge: no edition found in Mignet (1845), in the CODOIN or in recent work on the San Román collection; Gregorio Marañón’s Antonio Pérez (1947), with its documentary appendices, could not be checked. Rule applied: Daniel Bourdeau’s, 95% of the words read from the sense. Cipher part: 70 words; certain 60 (85.7%), probable {x} 9 (12.9%), restored [x] 0, unresolved ‹…› 1 (1.4%); read from the sense: 69/70 = 98.6%.

Conventions: {x} = probable reading; ‹…› = unresolved; Pérez’s plain text around the cipher is in grey. Spelling of the cipher kept; punctuation and accents added in the plain text only.

Established text

[…] el despacho que lleva este correo, pero con grandissima dificultad del consejo de hazienda, por no aver un real y tantas cosas que proveer , por lo qual […]

[…] quando no huviesse otras causas, {ir} acomodado {esso} de alguna {manera} que se {pueda} {estragar}, temiendo el peligro de los sucesos, estando lo de la hazienda tan {estrecho} que tengo por {imposible} del poderse acudir con tanto como es menester , y advierto a V. Al. […]

[…] la aceptación que el consejo de hazienda ha hecho deste assiento ha sido con protesto de que no se {cunplira} ‹ningun› otro, y que asi me ha {dicho} . Lo advierto a V. Al. […]

Translation

[…] but with the greatest difficulty on the part of the Council of Finance, since there is not a single real and so many things to provide for [in plain text: for which reason …]

[In plain text: … even if there were no other reasons,] to go and arrange this in some way that may be spoiled (?), for fear of the danger of events, the finances being so tight that I hold it impossible to be able to supply as much as is needed [in plain text: and I warn Your Highness …].

[In plain text: … the acceptance that the Council of Finance has made of this asiento] has been made under protest that no ‹other› will be honoured, and so I have been told [in plain text: I point this out to Your Highness].

Reading notes

  1. The cipher. It is neither Pérez’s cipher with Vargas Mexía (1578–1579) nor the “general cipher” of Don John and Escobedo (1576–1577): it is the numerical syllabary found in 1577 in the dispatches of the Spanish embassy at Genoa (Simancas, Estado, leg. 1410), with departures peculiar to Pérez. A draft of 4 February 1577 (Estado 1410,196) announces to the ministers in Italy the change of the “cifra general”; it does not contain the table.
  2. {ir}. The first sign of the second passage is blotted; the 2 (= i) and the superscript ˇ (= r) can be seen. We keep “ir acomodado”, as the cipher spells it.
  3. {estrecho}, {dicho}: “7 + hook”. A barred 7 followed by a hook stands for cho both times, as the words require; the sign is not attested elsewhere.
  4. {imposible}: sign 14. “por 14 16 po si 8²”: 16 = m, 8² = ble, so 14 is i here (in the Genoa table, 14 = gu). A single occurrence: probable reading.
  5. {cunplira}. The 7ı carries an oblique superscript stroke, which we read as ^ (= n); “no se cunplira” is required by “con protesto de que”.
  6. ‹ningun›. The signs give u-cin-gan (or nin-gan if 1 and 7 form 17). “ningun otro” is expected, but gan contradicts the u: we leave the word unresolved.
  7. {estragar}. The letters s-t-ra-ga-r are certain (8 = g in Pérez’s hand); the exact sense of the verb in the sentence remains uncertain.
  8. Prior work. Checked: Daniel Bourdeau’s cyphersolver repository, Cryptoole/Cryptiana (S. Tomokiyo), F. Mignet (1845), the CODOIN (full text, Internet Archive), P. Ávila Seoane (Vegueta, 2024, on Don John’s autographs in the same collection). Not checked: G. Marañón, Antonio Pérez (1947), whose appendices print many of Pérez’s letters; if the letter is edited there, the present reading becomes an independent check of it.

Method, validation and credits

Method (protocol written and hashed before any computation, three amendments, three sessions): (1) neutral transcription of the signs, frozen (SHA-256). (2) The system was recognised as that of the 1577 Genoa cipher dispatches, whose table we had rebuilt on cipher / “descifrada” pairs from Simancas; Pérez’s key K_P derives from it. (3) A first lexical test did not separate the true key from the controls (a syllabary yields words even when shuffled): we declared it inconclusive. (4) Pair validation: on Estado 1410,69–70, 72.4% of the words of the contemporary decipherment recovered (75% threshold missed). Diagnosis after the measurement: 27 is x/s, not f. (5) Decisive validation on a fresh pair, Estado 1410,65–66 (Genoa, 19 July 1577): key K_P2 (= K_P + 27 = x) frozen (SHA-256 4d5eb01d…), twelve lines of the cipher transcribed in two passes and frozen before the “descifrada” was opened; words containing 8 (b in the Genoa table, g in Pérez’s hand) excluded in advance. Result: 81.3% of the words and 87.9% of the characters of the contemporary decipherment recovered, against at best 16.5% and 47.8% for 200 control keys. (6) Reading of Pérez’s letter with K_P2, doubtful signs checked on the full-resolution images.

Credits. Document and image: Real Academia de la Historia, Biblioteca Digital, 2/Ms Caja 8 nº 4, images (Public Domain Mark 1.0). Validation pair: Ministerio de Cultura (España), Archivo General de Simancas, Estado 1410,65–66, PARES (images not reproduced). Transcription, decipherment, text, translations and notes: Brice Dudout, with Claude (Anthropic), October 2026.

General Rubio Navarrete to the Ministry of War: three telegrams in “Clave núm. 109”, 1913–1914

Mexico, 1913–1914. After the coup of February 1913, General Victoriano Huerta’s federal army fought Venustiano Carranza’s Constitutionalists. General Guillermo Rubio Navarrete commanded first in the Northeast (Lampazos, Nuevo León, summer 1913), against Pablo González’s troops, then at Zacatecas in the spring of 1914, as Villa marched on Torreón. His drafts of telegrams to the Minister of War are partly in cipher, in the “Clave núm. 109” that the Secretaría de Guerra y Marina had issued to him; the key sheet stayed among his papers. The cipher passages carry what he would not entrust to the telegraph clerks: the Laredo garrison courted by the Carrancistas, an old federal general in touch with the revolutionaries at San Antonio, Texas, and the lack of material and men to reopen the railway to Torreón.

Dates 18 July 1913, 13 March 1914, 18 March 1914; signed drafts, the first incomplete
Places Lampazos (Nuevo León) → Mexico City; Zacatecas → Mexico City
Sender Guillermo Rubio Navarrete, general of the federal army
Recipient the Minister (Secretary) of War and Navy, Mexico City
Source Centro de Estudios de Historia de México (CEHM-Carso, Fundación Carlos Slim), fondo DLXXIII (Manuscritos del General Guillermo Rubio Navarrete), DLXXIII.1.30.16-49, 2.41.9-41 and 2.41.13-41. The key: DLXXIII.1.28.14-23.
Cipher “Clave núm. 109. Secretaría de Guerra y Marina, con el General Guillermo Rubio Navarrete”: a printed table of 160 numbers. Letters (1–3 u, 13–15 o, 25–27 i, 37–39 e, 49–51 a, then 61 d to 93 z), syllables (pa, pe… ta, te, ti) and military words (98 Gobernador, 106 tropa, 107 fuerza, 112 vía, 132 General…). The numbers are set in the plain text, joined by dashes

Keywords guarnicion laredo · carrancismo · san antonio texas · reconstruccion de la via · a torreon

CEHM records (images in the CEHM viewer) ↗
Daniel Bourdeau’s catalogue, no. 1468 ↗

State of the reading. First published decipherment, to our knowledge: nothing in the cyphersolver repository, in Cryptiana or in Roberto Narváez’s open-access articles; his book Criptografía diplomática, política y militar en México 1813-1926 (SRE, 2019) could not be consulted. Rule applied: Daniel Bourdeau’s, 95% of the words read from the sense. Cipher parts of the three telegrams: 67 words; certain 64 (95.5%), probable {x} 3 (4.5%), restored [x] 0, unresolved 0; read from the sense: 67/67 = 100%.

Conventions: the telegram’s plain text is in grey, the decipherment in black; {x} = probable reading. Spelling of the cipher kept (“teellez”, “sobemanera”, “envia”, “plza”); accents added in the plain text only.

Established text

Lampazos, 18 July 1913, to the Minister of War and Navy (DLXXIII.1.30.16-49, incomplete)

Hónrame comunicar a Ud. personas de confianza me informan que guarnicion laredo es muy solicitada por carrancismo y que jefe de la plaza no merece toda confianza , así como que general treviño está en san antonio texas en relaciones con revolucionarios. Permítome indicar conveniencia de la estancia del Sr. Gral. teellez en laredo , así como mandar persona de confianza a san antonio , pues general treviño por su edad se ha hecho muy maleable y siempre está de acuerdo con la última persona con quien habla. En la entrevista que […]

[Zacatecas], 13 March 1914, to the Secretary of War (DLXXIII.2.41.9-41)

Hónrome participar a Ud. que unicamente espero {material} y fuerzas para comenzar la reconstruccion de la via que esta terminada en dos meses . Respetuosamente. Gral. de División G. Rubio.

[Zacatecas], 18 March 1914, to the Minister of War (DLXXIII.2.41.13-41)

Me es honroso participar a usted con toda atención que urge sobemanera el envia de fuerzas a esta {plza} , pues con el solo anuncio de que vengo a reparar la vía a torreon los rebeldes se estan dedicando con gran actividad a {destruirla} totalmente, lo que es imposible evitar con el escaso efectivo de fuerzas que existen en esta . Respetuosamente. G. Rubio.

Translation

Lampazos, 18 July 1913, to the Minister of War and Navy (DLXXIII.1.30.16-49, incomplete)

I have the honour to inform you that persons I trust tell me that the Laredo garrison is much courted by Carrancismo and that the commander of the place does not deserve full trust; also that General Treviño is at San Antonio, Texas, in relations with revolutionaries. I venture to point out that General Téllez should stay at Laredo, and that a trusted person should be sent to San Antonio, since General Treviño, because of his age, has become very pliable and always agrees with the last person he talks to. In the interview that […]

[Zacatecas], 13 March 1914, to the Secretary of War (DLXXIII.2.41.9-41)

I have the honour to inform you that I am only waiting for material and troops to begin the reconstruction of the railway, which will be finished in two months. Respectfully, General of Division G. Rubio.

[Zacatecas], 18 March 1914, to the Minister of War (DLXXIII.2.41.13-41)

I have the honour to inform you, with all respect, that it is extremely urgent to send troops to this place, for at the mere announcement that I am coming to repair the railway to Torreón, the rebels are setting about destroying it completely with great activity, which it is impossible to prevent with the small number of troops that there are in this [place]. Respectfully, G. Rubio.

Reading notes

  1. The key. The printed sheet of “Clave núm. 109”, in Rubio Navarrete’s name, is filed with his telegrams (DLXXIII.1.28.14-23). Every number of the three telegrams is on it; no value was added or corrected.
  2. Validation by a contemporary pair. The typed telegram of 30 March 1914 (DLXXIII.2.41.18-41) has its pencil draft (DLXXIII.1.29.9-30), on which Rubio wrote the plain text above the numbers: “… la ha dado guarnición de dicha plaza por conferencia tenida hoy. Espero fuerzas”. The key, frozen before the measurement, gives back this plain text 100% (see Method). The rest of the cipher in the same telegram, with no contemporary plain text, reads “para poder seguir mis trabajos al norte”.
  3. {material} (13 March 1914): the second 159 (te) is badly formed; the value is required by “ma-te-ri-a-l”.
  4. {plza} (18 March 1914): group 93 (z) is written over another figure; the cipher gives “p-l-z-a” without the second a, which we do not restore.
  5. {destruirla}: the middle figure of 153 (ru) is under the CEHM watermark; “de-s-t-ru-i-r-la” is required by the sense.
  6. Spelling. “teellez” (te-e-ll-e-z: Téllez), “sobemanera” (the r of sobre omitted), “envia” (en + vía, for envío): we keep the spelling of the cipher.
  7. The people. General Joaquín Téllez commanded the federal forces in the Northeast; the elderly “General Treviño” at San Antonio is probably Gerónimo Treviño (born 1836), former military chief of the Northeast under Porfirio Díaz (identification not checked in the sources).
  8. The rest of the fonds. The other “en clave” pieces of no. 1468 use other tables: an alphabetical numerical syllabary from 1 to 255 for the traffic with Téllez and the División del Bravo (a draft of 19 July 1913, DLXXIII.1.30.17-49, carries a pencil interlinear decipherment), a two-figure code (DLXXIII.1.30.5-49, 1.30.27-49), a presidential code (1.31.29-30, 2.41.17-41, 2.41.19-41) and a “Clave nº 99” (2.41.1-41). These tables are not in the file; those pieces are not read here.

Method, validation and credits

Method (protocol written and hashed before any decoding, SHA-256 98f394ad…): (1) transcription of the key sheet, frozen (SHA-256 9adb1190…) before any telegram was opened; (2) validation on the contemporary pair of 30 March 1914 (typed telegram DLXXIII.2.41.18-41 ↔ draft with plain text, DLXXIII.1.29.9-30): the first ten groups, checked by eye before the protocol, are excluded; on the held-out part (9 words) the key gives 100% of the characters and 100% of the words, against at best −0.02 and 11% for 200 control keys (table values permuted); thresholds 0.85 / 0.75; (3) transcription of each telegram, frozen before decoding; (4) mechanical decoding, doubtful figures checked on the image.

Credits. Documents: Centro de Estudios de Historia de México (CEHM-Carso), Fundación Carlos Slim, fondo DLXXIII, records 1.30.16-49, 2.41.9-41, 2.41.13-41 (images not reproduced). Lead: Daniel Bourdeau’s catalogue, no. 1468. Transcription, decipherment, text, translations and notes: Brice Dudout, with Claude (Anthropic), October 2026.

Melchiorre Biglia, nuncio in Vienna: “mal principio al negociare”, [5] December 1565

Vienna, late 1565. Melchiorre Biglia, sent by Pius IV as nuncio to Emperor Maximilian II, is conducting a difficult negotiation: the Emperor asks for the right of priests in his lands to marry (the “connubio”), which Rome refuses; in return the Pope offers military help against the Turk. The register of Biglia’s letters at the Ambrosiana holds two letters entirely in cipher, never published (Dengel, who edited the nunciature in 1926, prints nothing of them). We publish the second one here. Biglia answers the reproaches he received from Rome for a “bad start” to the negotiation that offended the Emperor; he discusses the offer of four thousand foot or two thousand horse, advises that the Emperor send “a person of his blood” at their head, and recounts the visit of Doctors Zasius and Weber, of the privy council, who came to dine with him.

Date “a li [cinque] di decembre del sesanta [cinque]”: December 1565; the day (5?) is restored, not read
Place Vienna (“uiena”) → Rome
Sender Melchiorre Biglia, apostolic nuncio to Maximilian II
Recipient not named in the cipher; “V.S.” (restored reading), probably a cardinal of the Curia
Source Milan, Veneranda Biblioteca Ambrosiana, Trotti 22, fol. 7r lines 33–45 and fol. 7v lines 1–23 (register of Biglia’s letters; digitised by the Università Cattolica, no reuse licence: no image reproduced).
Cipher numerical syllabic cipher written without spaces, words separated by “00”: a single digit = vowel or bare consonant (2 e/s, 3 u/l, 4 i/t, 5 a/n, 7 o/r); two digits = row consonant (0 m/g/v, 1 c/p, 2 s, 3 l, 4 t, 5 n, 6 d/f, 7 r, 8 soft c/b, 9 gn) + column vowel (1/2/8 e, 3 u, 4/6 i, 5 a, 7/9 o); codes 59 qua, 97 che, 19 per; a small nomenclator (11 S.M., 9 e, 49 non, 3 questo, 4 quel, 87 connubio, 21 Imperatore)

Key words mal principio al negociare · quatro milia fanti ouero due mila cauali · persona di suo sangue per capo · il dotore Ciasio e il dotore Vueber · il particolare del connubio

Daniel Bourdeau’s catalogue, no. 1338 ↗

State of the reading. Partial reading, explained; unpublished to our knowledge (Dengel, Nuntiaturberichte aus Deutschland II/5, 1926, uses this register but prints neither cipher; online search negative). Rule applied: Daniel Bourdeau’s, 95% of words read by sense, counted per letter. This letter: 381 cipher words; sure 313, probable {x} 42, restored [x] 7, unresolved ‹…› 19; read (sure + probable): 355/381 = 93.2%, below the threshold (95.0% with the restored words). The first letter (fols 6v–7r, 729 words) stands at 94.5% and is not published.

Conventions: {x} = probable reading; [x] = restored from the sense; ‹…› = cipher word not read. Spelling of the cipher kept (single consonants: “ofeso”, “cauali”, “afetione”, “dotore”). One line = one line of the manuscript.

Established text

7r 33 le {riprensioni} che [V.S.] mi a di qua dato mal {principio} al negociare

7r 34 e che S.M. sia restato ofeso io le riceuo in loco di amoreuole

7r 35 ricordo e ne le rendo quel gratie che io poso {magiori ma}

7r 36 e gia uolunta di {piu} tosto morire che di ofendere {S.M. questo}

7r 37 {e} quel {di} che io piu fo caso che di quanto {male} poteuami

7r 41 afermarli che io ueramente ‹…› quel ‹…› le ‹…›

7r 42 ‹…› dele quali sono {ripreso} di cio {transgreso} e circa

7r 44 a questo ‹…› mostro ben una poca satisfacione uerso

7r 45 il ‹…› quanto sia ala oferta deli quatro milia fanti

7v 2 ‹…› se la eletione deli quatro mila fanti a ‹…›

7v 3 gia ‹…› liberta a S.M. di elegere li capi di esi

7v 4 fanti et di farli o li fanti ouero li cauali e

7v 5 che S.M. posa elegere li cauali di quel [nationi] che le piacera {e per}

7v 6 confirmatione di cio io disi al S.M. che io {credera} che {S.M. douese}

7v 7 mandare persona di suo sangue per capo di esi per meglio

7v 8 dimostrarli la molta afetione che le porto io non ‹…›

7v 9 piu di ‹…› che io certifico [V.S.] non ci e fundo da dubitare

7v 11 uoluto et fuse dato ieri furno a {pransare meco}

7v 15 che li a e uenendo {al} particolare del connubio {disero che}

7v 23 {di} uiena {a li} [cinque] di {decembre} del {sesanta} [cinque] ‹…›

Translation

The {reproofs} that [Your Lordship] sends me — that I have made a bad {beginning} of the negotiation here, and that His Majesty has remained offended — I receive as a loving reminder, and I give you for them the greatest thanks I can; {but} my will is already to die {rather} than offend {His Majesty}: {this} is what I care for most, more than any {harm} that could befall me ‹…›, and it is what burns and torments my soul. I can do nothing now but {beg} ‹…› ‹…›; for my part I {shall} also do this: take care to assure {His Majesty} that truly ‹…› ‹…› ‹…› for which I am {reproved} and in which I would have {erred}.

As to the connubio, I know well that, if he {remains} satisfied with {His Majesty}, to this ‹…› shows very little satisfaction towards the ‹…›. As to the offer of four thousand foot or two thousand horse, I certainly {can} ‹…› ‹…› {offering} ‹…› that, if the choice of the four thousand foot ‹…›, ‹…› freedom to His Majesty to choose their captains, and to raise either the foot or the horse, and that His Majesty may choose the horse of whatever [nation] he pleases. {And in} confirmation I told His Majesty that I {would think} that {His Majesty should} send a person of his own blood as their head, the better to show them the great affection I bear him. I do not ‹…› more of ‹…›, for I certify to [Your Lordship] that there is no ground to fear a greater loss than the offer that {His Majesty would have} wanted {would have} cost, had it been made.

Yesterday Doctor {Ciasio} and Doctor {Vueber} of the {privy council} [Zasius and Weber] came {to dine with me}; withdrawn with me into my room, they assured me of the great affection and devotion borne to His Majesty and of the {great obligation} owed him; and, coming {to} the particular of the connubio, they {said that}, if one wished to ask it in good heart, he can only be content with what pleases His Majesty, knowing well that to please you he will do all he {can}, for the many loving {demonstrations} that have been ‹…›; and in particular [they] told [me] that he will never consent to anything against the {authority} of His Majesty; and they themselves offer themselves as most devoted servants of His Majesty. ‹…›

{From} Vienna, [the fifth] of {December}, [fifteen] {sixty}-[five]. ‹…›

Reading notes

  1. S.M. (code 11, sure: ≥ 3 contexts) designates the Emperor; its exact wording (“S.M.”, “l’imperatore”) cannot be decided. Code 21, which is se by the key, also bears the value Imperatore in the first letter (polyphony declared before reading); it does not occur here.
  2. [V.S.] (code 45, in by the key): value restored from the sense; the recipient is not named.
  3. {S.M. questo} (7r 36): two nomenclator codes written without a separator (11 + 3); 3 = questo is always followed by “000”, as here.
  4. {ofrendo} (7v 1) and {molto obligo} (7v 14) assume the bare values 6 = f and 8 = b, which are not in the validated key: probable readings only.
  5. Ciasio and Vueber are read exactly; their identification with Johann Ulrich Zasius and Johann Baptist Weber, Maximilian II’s councillors whom Delfino recommended to Commendone as “consiglieri primarii”, is probable (Dengel, NB II/5).
  6. The connubio: marriage of priests, which Maximilian II asked of Rome; Dengel (NB II/5, introduction) recalls that the Emperor hoped to obtain it until the death of Pius IV on 9 December 1565.
  7. The date: “uiena” and “di decembre del {sesanta}” are read; code 14569, twice, is restored [cinque] only from the year 1565 given by the neighbouring plain-text letters (15/11/1565 before, 16/1/1566 after). The day is not established. 7v 22 ends with an isolated word (1886) that is not read, and the date with another (10869).
  8. Re-reading of the image: 7v 22–23, the short line ending the text stops after “1886”; “64” (di) opens the date line (probable reading).

Method, validation and credits

Method (protocol written before any computation). (1) Key rebuilt from the ciphertext alone (sessions C03–C05): a solver on a training part (L1 6v–7r line 2 and this letter), then refinement by hand; key K5d frozen (SHA-256 50f9f337…). (2) Validation on a held-out portion, never decoded before (L1, 7r lines 3–27, 1,543 digits): lexical agreement 0.761 against at most 0.500 for 200 controls (threshold fixed in advance: 0.65), with a spelling normalisation (v/u, j/i, h, double consonants) fixed before the measurement. A loader bug found afterwards dropped a few digits at line ends: it worked against the key, so the validation stands. (3) Word-by-word reading, frozen before counting; “sure” = exact output of the validated key (checked by program); any value taken from context (bare values 1 = c/p, 6 = f, 8 = b, joined codes) is counted probable; a nomenclator word is sure only with three independent contexts. (4) The 75 words still unread after session C07 were re-read one by one on the image before being decoded again; corrections made this way remain probable.

Decipherment: Brice Dudout, with Claude (Anthropic), October 2026. Item reported by: Daniel Bourdeau, cyphersolver catalogue no. 1338. Historical context: H. Dengel, Nuntiaturberichte aus Deutschland II/5 (Vienna, 1926). Manuscript: Veneranda Biblioteca Ambrosiana, Trotti 22 (consulted on the digital library of the Università Cattolica).

The Cardinal of Tortosa to Charles V: the paragraph that “could not be translated”, Valladolid, 9 September 1520

On 9 September 1520 Adrian of Utrecht – Cardinal of Tortosa, regent of Castile for Charles V, and sixteen months later Pope Adrian VI – wrote from Valladolid while the Junta of the Comunidades was settling at Ávila. In the middle of the letter are six lines in cipher. Danvila, who printed the letter in 1897, noted only: “Sigue un párrafo cifrado que no ha podido traducirse”. The cipher is the Cardinal’s dotted code; we rebuilt it from his other letters of 1520–1521 whose plain text is known, validated it on a letter held out, and applied it to this paragraph. It tells what the Junta meant to do to the grandees: take from them the alcabalas and the towns that had belonged to the Crown. Update of 9 November 2026: on a lead from Daniel Bourdeau, the cipher sheet PTR,LEG,2,1,100 fol. 434 gave three more words; the reading rises from 87.0% to 93.5%, still below the 95% threshold.

Date 9 September 1520 (“En Valladolid a ix de Setiembre de mil quinientos y veynte”)
Place Valladolid → Charles V, then in the Low Countries
Sender Adrian of Utrecht, Cardinal of Tortosa, governor of Castile (signed “Vre tres humble serviteur, Car.l dertusen.”)
Recipient Charles V, King of Castile and Emperor-elect
Source Archivo General de Simancas, Patronato Real, PTR,LEG,2,1,19, f. 1r (PARES 12987122); formerly “Comunidades de Castilla, leg. 2, fols. 157–158”. Letter printed without the cipher paragraph by A. Danvila, Historia crítica y documentada de las Comunidades de Castilla, in Memorial histórico español XXXVI (1897), pp. 17–19.
Cipher the Cardinal’s “dotted trigraph” code: consonant-vowel-consonant groups followed by a dot for words and syllables (gig. que, leb. no, sa. de, nof. los, mud. -mente…), and a homophonic alphabet of signs (h, ð, M = e; cf, 4, g, B× = a; ⊥, φ = r; y̥, p = s; ε̥ = t…). The same code in the letters of 1520 and 1521 (PTR,LEG,2,1,23, 30, 32, 61, 68, 70, 71, 73, 85, 88, 99)

Keywords contra todos los grandes · todas las alcavalas · las villas y lugares · de la corona real

Record and images (PARES) ↗
Danvila, MHE XXXVI ↗
Daniel Bourdeau: the joint letter of 30 December 1521 (another code) ↗

State of the reading. Partial reading, explained; unpublished to our knowledge. Rule applied: Daniel Bourdeau’s, 95% of words read for sense. Of 46 cipher words (the two plain words “quanto mas” excluded; “dels” counted as one word): 28 certain (60.9%), 15 probable {x} (32.6%), 2 restored from the sense [x] (4.3%), 1 unresolved ‹…› (2.2%); read (certain + probable): 43 / 46 = 93.5% (45 / 46 = 97.8% with the restored words, which do not count as read). Below the 95% threshold (44 words would be needed): this is not a complete decipherment. Each probable, restored or unresolved word is justified below. Keys: K7, validated on 2 November 2026 on a held-out letter (see “Method”); three words ({Quiça}, {quitar}, {villas}) are read with the derived key K7b (K7 + 18 entries learnt from fol. 434, 9 November 2026), declared and not re-validated: they stay probable. Before the update of 9 November: 28 certain, 12 probable, 4 restored, 2 unresolved (40 / 46 = 87.0%).

Conventions: {x} = probable reading; ‹…› = unresolved; [x] = restored from the sense. Spelling of the cipher; punctuation and accents added sparingly.

Plain-text context (same letter)

En Plazencia tanbien han quitado al corregidor la vara […] y dixieronle que si muchas mas recibiera por vra. Mat. todas ie las tomaran | el fin que sobresto tienen sabra v. al. por la cifra que va dentro desta | quanto mas

Established text

{Quiça} esto dara ‹fud.› a estos [tales], que no {solamente} se mueuen {contra} [vuestra] magestad, {mas} ahun contra todos los grandes, dels quales {entienden} {primeramente} {quitar} todas las {alcavalas}, y {despues} todas las {villas} {y} lugares que de {poco} {tiempo} en {fueron} de la {corona} real.

Translation

“… and all the more {perhaps} this will give ‹…› to these [men], who rise not {only} {against} [Your] Majesty {but} also against all the grandees, from whom they {intend} {first} to {take away} all the {alcabalas}, {and then} all the {towns} {and} places which {lately} {were} of the royal {Crown}.”

Justification of the probable, restored and unresolved words

  1. dara (certain): o̥o = d, 9 = a, ꞡ = r, cf = a, all firm values of key K7; “esto dará”.
  2. {solamente}: ded. = “sola”, a single attestation, followed by mud. = -mente (certain).
  3. {contra} (l. 2): vuh. = con and ε̥ = t certain, then a ⊥ with o below that is not in the key, and 4 = a: “cont‹?›a”.
  4. {mas}: nah. = mas, a single attestation.
  5. {entienden}: zu. = “entende”, a single attestation (PTR,LEG,2,1,73, “da allá en que entender”), + & = n.
  6. {primeramente}: p r i ‹?› e r a + mud. (-mente); the 4th sign (ʆ) is r or t in the key, not m.
  7. {alcavalas}: 8 of 9 signs have firm values; the 3rd (z with a stroke above) is not attested for c.
  8. {despues}: su. = des (firm), then gad. = pues, a single attestation.
  9. {y} (l. 5): the sign n = y has a single attestation.
  10. {poco} {tiempo}: hag. and cu., one attestation each, in the letter of 15 March 1521 (PTR,LEG,2,1,68) and its contemporary transcription (2,1,69): “hay pocos o ningunos que en este tiempo quieran comprar”.
  11. {fueron}: qec. = “fue”, a single attestation (2,1,73, “ha dias que fue a Burgos”), + r, o, n.
  12. {corona}: 5 of 6 signs certain; the key gives e for the 1st (ð), read c (shape close to θ = c); sense fixed by “real”.
  13. [tales]: “a estos ‹?›ales”; -ales certain, “estos tales” a common phrase; the first sign is an uninventoried shape.
  14. [vuestra]: “contra ‹q m.› mu.”; mu. = magestad (certain), elsewhere always preceded by a “vuestra” group (cim.); the two signs before it are outside the key.
  15. {Quiça} (9 November 2026, key K7b): the first word, tt Fx m mo th 4. In the cipher sheet fol. 434 (PTR,LEG,2,1,100) the pair tt + Fx (tt followed by the looped long s with a small o) is q six times (quitome, quise, quitaria, quiero, quatro, aqui), against Danvila’s printed plain text (MHE XXXVIII pp. 547-549); the shape was compared on the images (2,1,19 l. 1 against “quatro”). m = u, mo = i, th = c (firm in K7), 4 = a. Probable, not certain: the 5th sign is θ/ð, and ð = e would give “quiea”. “quanto mas quiça esto dara …”. The earlier reading “p ‹?› u i c a” (“publica”?) is dropped.
  16. {quitar} (9 November 2026, key K7b; replaces [juntar]): Qx dho Z q 4 gr. The 1st sign (the “odd g” of Brice Dudout’s re-reading) has the shape of the barred q with an S-shaped tail of “quitaciones” in fol. 434 (one attestation); dho = u (one attestation in K7), q = t, 4 = a, gr = r. Z is n in K7 but i in fol. 434 (“diga”), and the shape is ambiguous i/c/n in the sign atlas; “q u n t a r” is no word. “primeramente quitar todas las alcavalas y despues todas las villas”: taking the alcabalas and the towns from the grandees, a Comuneros’ demand, fits better than “juntar” (gather).
  17. {villas} (9 November 2026, key K7b; was [villas], restored): oto ‹ti› b g9 p. The sign transcribed “ti” is the Ꝉ-shaped Li = i (firm in K7; the same shape as in “publicamente”, fol. 434). The plain b has the shape of the b = ll of “allego” (fol. 434, one attestation); the barred b (ƀ) of fol. 434 is z (haziendas, four times), a different sign, hence the split b = ll / ƀ = z in K7b. u i ll a s = “villas”, with “villas y lugares”.
  18. Unresolved: the group fud., without value in K7 or K7b and absent from fol. 434 (where ful. = secreta is attested twice, fud. never). Suggestion, not counted: a noun meaning “boldness” or “occasion” (“esto dara ánimo / ocasión a estos tales”); nothing proves it. The phrase “de poco tiempo en fueron” is awkward; the group zi. = en is certain.

Historical notes

  1. The moment. In August–September 1520 the Junta of the Comunidades, meeting at Ávila, seized Tordesillas (29 August) and Queen Joanna; Adrian, at Valladolid, tried in vain to draw it to the town (the mission of the commander Hinestrosa, told in plain text in the letter). The cipher paragraph gives the rest of the Junta’s programme against the grandees.
  2. Alcabalas and Crown towns. Abolishing or reducing the alcabalas (the sales tax) and returning to the Crown the towns and places alienated to lords were among the Comuneros’ demands; the contemporary transcription of the Cardinal’s letters of 21 March 1521 still speaks of “cosas enajenadas de la corona”.
  3. “La cifra que va dentro desta”. The paragraph follows the plain sentence “el fin que sobresto tienen sabrá V. Al. por la cifra que va dentro desta”. An enclosed cipher sheet therefore existed; its contemporary decipherment survives separately (PTR,LEG,2,1,107: the Junta means to take the title of king from Charles during the Queen’s lifetime, according to the Marquis of Villena’s secretary). It is not the text of the paragraph read here.
  4. The Cardinal’s other letters. Almost all his cipher letters of 1520–1521 are printed deciphered by Danvila, from the contemporary transcriptions. Still without plain text: this paragraph and a struck-out cipher paragraph of 21 October 1520. The sheet wholly in cipher enclosed with the letter of 7 December 1521 (PTR,LEG,2,1,100, fol. 434), whose decipherment Danvila says “puede pertenecer á otra”, is in fact the cipher original of the paragraphs of the letter from Vitoria of 24 October 1521, which Danvila prints deciphered (MHE XXXVIII, p. 547) from the contemporary transcription (PTR,LEG,2,1,92): key K7 reads its first line “… apareiamos … exercito … mas muy …”. The joint letter of 30 December 1521 (Estado 8,150), in another code, was re-read by Daniel Bourdeau on Gredilla’s decipherment.
  5. Update of 9 November 2026: fol. 434. On a lead from Daniel Bourdeau (7 November), the cipher sheet PTR,LEG,2,1,100 fol. 434 (three pages, 98 lines) was transcribed by shape and frozen, decoded mechanically with K7 frozen, and only then compared with Danvila’s printed decipherment (MHE XXXVIII pp. 547-549). K7 reads it almost word for word (“Acá aparejamos otra vez exercito mas muy a passo para que de muchos se diga publicamente …”). As this pair is an existing decipherment, and a few lines of Danvila had been seen earlier, it serves as training, not validation: no score is given. It yielded 18 entries (derived key K7b: 17 new labels, and K7’s b = z split into b = ll and ƀ = z), which give {Quiça}, {quitar} and {villas}.

Method, validation and credits

Method: (1) protocol written before any computation, with dated amendments; (2) key rebuilt from the Cardinal’s other cipher letters whose plain text is known: 8 October, 13 and 17 November 1520 (PTR,LEG,2,1,23, 30, 32 ↔ Bergenroth, CSP Spain, supplement of 1868, and Danvila), 23 February, 15 and 28 March, 8 and 30 August 1521 (2,1,61, 68, 70, 71, 73, 85, 88 ↔ Danvila or the contemporary transcriptions 2,1,69, 72, 83); code groups kept only when attested twice; (3) sign shapes re-read blind by Brice Dudout on three plates (pick the shape seen, no value shown), which separated confused homophones (9 / ꞡ, φ / ꝗ, ʒ / Ƶ…); (4) validation: a single measurement per fresh pair named before download, criterion fixed in advance (character agreement ≥ 0.85 and ≥ the best of 200 shuffled-key controls + 0.30; word agreement reported). A first version of this card (28 October, key K3: 0.851 of characters but 0.541 of words on 2,1,68) was withdrawn the same day; keys K4 (0.783 on 2,1,85) and K6 (0.813 on 2,1,88) failed, and those pairs then went into training. Key K7 is validated on the fresh pair 2,1,99 (letter from Vitoria, 5 December 1521, second cipher passage, ten lines transcribed and frozen before any reading of the plain text) against the plain text printed by Danvila (MHE XXXVIII, same letter): 0.882 of characters (n = 170) against at best 0.176 for 200 controls (median 0.041), rank 1/201; words 0.770 (controls ≤ 0.119). Thirteen tokens of 254 were left out of the score: abbreviations, and the plain-text words glimpsed while locating the letter (exclusion declared before transcription). (5) Reading of the 9 September paragraph with K7, on a sign transcription frozen before the measurement, and count under Daniel’s rule. (6) 9 November 2026: training on fol. 434 (see Notes), derived key K7b, not re-validated (no fresh pair was measured with it); the words that only it can read stay probable. All SHA-256 fingerprints are in the working folder.

Longlée to Henry IV: duplicate of a dispatch from Madrid, [December 1589 – February 1590] — partial reading

Pierre de Ségusson, sieur de Longlée, the French resident at Madrid, wrote in cipher to Henry IV early in 1590. The packet was intercepted: its copy, “Dupp. d’une despesche”, is now in the Biblioteca Nacional de España, with two other letters of Longlée that the Spaniards had deciphered by Luis Valle de la Cerda. Those two letters (3 March and 1 April 1590) were edited by Albert Mousset in 1912 from the originals at the French Foreign Office; this one was not, and no contemporary decipherment accompanies the copy. We publish the reading as far as we could take it, gaps included: 86.3% of the words, below the 95% threshold we hold ourselves to. It shows an envoy of the Duke of Mercœur at Madrid asking that Philip II declare openly against Henry IV and seize the goods of royalist Frenchmen.

Date undated; between December 1589 and February 1590: Longlée has had no dispatch from the King “depuis le troisiesme de nouembre”, and an envoy arrived “le vingtuniesme de ce mois”. Probably the duplicate of the dispatch of 25 February 1590, cited in the letter of 12 March 1590 (Mousset 1912), whose original is missing from the Foreign Office archives
Place Madrid → Henry IV (the duplicate goes by Bayonne)
Sender Pierre de Ségusson, sieur de Longlée, French resident with Philip II
Recipient Henry IV (“Vre Mate”); on the back of the bundle: “a Monsr. de Vendosme Principe de Bearne, que despues fue Rey de Francia”
Source Madrid, Biblioteca Nacional de España, Mss/994, item 6, ff. 67r–67v (“Dupp. d’une despesche”); study images DECODE R2253 (views 4 and 5), not reproduced. Ff. 64–65v and 68–69 of the same volume are the letters of 1 April and 3 March 1590, edited by A. Mousset, Dépêches diplomatiques de M. de Longlée, résident de France en Espagne (1582-1590), Paris, 1912, pp. 394–396 and 390–392, from the originals (AE, Mémoires et documents, Espagne 237)
Cipher Longlée’s nomenclator: an alphabet of homophonic signs (letters, digits, symbols) and a few signs for short words; the same hand as the two edited letters of the volume. Starting point: the table printed by Mousset (pp. lviii–lix), corrected on the hand of these copies

Keywords le dupplicata de ma derniere despeche · le duc de Mercure · leurs personnes biens marchandises et nauires · la defence de l’eglise catholique
