Letter no. 1388 — Montréal, 8 April 1759

My Lord,

In the letters I had the honour to write to you in cipher last autumn, I set out to give you as exact an account as I could of the sad state to which this colony was reduced. What followed has proved to me only too well that it was even more critical than I had had the honour to tell you. Day by day its extreme want of everything and the most dreadful misery of the colonists have grown. Soon {there will be} no hope left of finding resources: horned cattle, domestic animals and horses are almost entirely gone. Several of the better-off inhabitants, my Lord, have only the animals of a single plough left; most of the others have none at all. These animals have served to make up for the bread cut from the troops; the people have only four ounces of bread a day and nothing else to live on.

The English are well aware of it; they {hasten} to seize so fine an opportunity to {invade} this colony. Food, munitions of war and everything else are as plentiful with them as we are short of them. The attacks they threaten us with seem most certain. It is no longer a question of the same forces they used in the previous campaigns: they are more than doubling them. They expect some resistance from us, they make no secret of it; nor do they make a secret that nothing will withstand their obstinacy and their fury.

I have lost no time in setting all the forces of this colony in motion. I have had a very exact census made of the three governments: that of Quebec will give me six {thousand} three hundred and fifty-six men; that of Montréal five thousand four hundred and fifty-five; that of Trois-Rivières one thousand three hundred and thirteen. And only the sick and those too old to serve will remain. From the number of militia fit for war one must even deduct the men indispensable for transport and the other needs of the service. We have besides the eight battalions of the land troops and the forty companies of the Marine troops, which are not complete.

I must, my Lord, provide:

1. for the {defen}ce of our frontier at Carillon, which will probably be attacked by twenty-five to thirty thousand men. You saw, my Lord, from my letters of last autumn, that my energy in relieving that side had obliged the English to give up the attack, {and} had even {hastened} their retreat. The Marquis de Montcalm could have made it extremely {difficult} for them, but although I wrote to him, and the Marine troops, the Canadians and the Indians showed him their wish to pursue the enemy, nothing could bring him round to my views.

2. for the {defen}ce of the Belle-Rivière [Ohio] against an army of about ten thousand men. I had foreseen the fate of Fort Duquesne. M. de Lignery, having had to reduce his force in proportion to his provisions, took the wisest course in evacuating and blowing up that fort as six to seven thousand English approached, and withdrawing to {Fort} Machault. He holds out there. I have the forces and other help near him to support him, but the thing seems very difficult.

3. for the {defen}ce of Niagara, which is to be besieged by ten thousand men. You have seen that this {post} and those of the Belle-Rivière are to help one another, and to give preference to the {defen}ce of Niagara as the main and most essential one, the key of the river of the upper country. By this arrangement I [...] that of our enemies, who want to join their army of the Ohio to the one they are to send to Niagara. M. Pouchot, captain in the Béarn regiment, is to take up the command there again. I have given him my instructions for every case; he will above all try to oppose the enemy's landing.

4. for the {defen}ce of La Présentation, to keep our communication on Lake Ontario, and to {set} limits to the very ambitious designs of our enemies, who announce ten thousand men for that side and want by that way to push on to Montréal with an even stronger army.

This winter I had two corvettes built, of ten twelve-pounders each, which will serve for the transports to Niagara and will manoeuvre as circumstances allow to {harass} the enemy. I have moreover set up a flying camp to watch the English and to be told of their movements on that lake. They want to re-establish Oswego and will employ ten thousand men on it. All things considered, I see the same plan reborn that the Duke of Cumberland conceived. General {Hamerts} [Amherst], who was his aide-de-camp, doubtless wants to make good General Braddock's failure.

Quebec too is threatened by forces incomparably greater than all those of this colony. The fortifications of that town need many repairs, and even outworks. For all these works four thousand men would be needed: where can they be found, and how fed, in this position? I have confined myself to having such materials prepared during the winter as could be gathered without causing any extraordinary {consumption} of food. M. de Pontleroy will stay in Quebec to carry on the most urgent works as far as our situation allows.

The safety of this capital much occupies those who do not share my views; from this come arguments and talk which creep in and gradually become public. But the objects I have in view are at this {moment} the most pressing. Indeed, my Lord, it is quite certain that our frontiers and the {posts} I mean to {defen}d will be attacked; it is even to be feared that most will give way to the enemy's too great superiority. But it is my policy to do my best to keep them; to abandon them would sound ill in every respect:

1. all our Indians, seeing no more Frenchmen, would find themselves obliged to join the English;

2. the English, no longer busy far away, would no longer be bound to hard and painful marches, or to finding means of easing and speeding the transport of the [...] of their army; they could unite and push forward rapidly as far as they liked;

3. finally, if we had peace, they would find themselves at little cost in {possession} of the {posts} we had evacuated, and so of the immense extent of country that depends on them.

It is not the same with Quebec. I {believe} indeed the English have an inordinate desire to conquer it. But 1. it is not at all certain that they have at will all they need for so important an expedition; 2. I must naturally {believe} myself assured [that] the King, having been informed by you, my Lord, of the insufficiency both of our forces and of our means, His Majesty, knowing of such an armament, will have been pleased to provide for opposing that enterprise; 3. supposing I had to {defen}d Quebec with the weak forces and small means [we have] at present, our enemies could not reach it without my being informed long before by the look-outs I have posted as far as the mouth of the river. Now, however diligent a fleet that sails with care may be, it cannot reach Quebec before the fate of the battle the English are to give us at Carillon is decided. Whatever the outcome of that battle, my Lord, I shall always keep the freedom to go to Quebec myself with most of our troops and all the militia and Indian nations I can gather in the three governments. I shall leave at Carillon only what is indispensable, and the armed xebecs. Once at Quebec I shall give the enemy battle, and do so again until I have forced him to withdraw, or until, overwhelmed by his excessive superiority, he has entirely reduced me. Given my determination to oppose the landing, [it] will be all the more in place since I should not have enough powder, bombs, shot etc. to sustain a siege for six days. If I have the success I hope for, I shall at once march all these [forces] to Carillon to stop the enemy there, or prevent him from wintering there if he had taken {possession} of it.

From all these considerations you see, my Lord, that the least change in my arrangements would have the most unfortunate consequences. If the English took Carillon and held it, they would make only too much of that advantage; they would make their mightiest efforts to break into the colony.

My position is a thorny one. However {well considered} my arrangements, I cannot, my Lord, guarantee you the outcome. I shall always do my best, I shall watch over everything, and it will be only to the insufficiency of my forces, the exhaustion of the colony's resources and the enemy's extreme superiority that he will owe his successes, if he has any.

Could I, my Lord, have stronger reasons to wish for the arrival, very early in the spring, 1. of the battalions I have had the honour to ask of you; 2. of munitions [...] etc.; 3. of food? This last object above all, though placed last, occupies [and] worries the colonists and the troops in general. I make it, my Lord, my most laborious industry and my constant care. I have taken from the Canadians even their own food; I have taken by {auth}ority all the meal of the mills; I appealed in the King's name, with the most urgent entreaties, to the tithes of the parish priests; the Bishop was good enough to help by his exhortations to those gentlemen. In spite of this I can so little hope to make up the provisions indispensable to take the field that M. Bigot has been forced to send {half} of these provisions down to Quebec to feed the people. We are {tota}lly short of goods. The Indian nations of the upper country in general suffer in their most urgent needs. The English do everything to win them over. Can I expect that the southern nations will come to Presqu'île and all the northern ones to this town? I dare not count on it. And if they came, could I keep them, being destitute of everything, and above all of {provisions}? They would probably {withdraw}; pressed by their needs, they would turn to the English, who, welcoming them, would get the same services from them as we do. I study the movements of the English and {prepare} everything to march our troops, militia and Indians {as soon} as I know they are on the way. If I sent them off too early, once their food was eaten I should have no means left at all. It is all the more to be wished that you have provided, my Lord, for sending the colony a supplement to the provisions asked for by M. Bigot and by the contractor, since most of our inhabitants have no grain to sow their fields.

Whatever state I may be reduced to, I shall never lack zeal or confidence for the defence of this colony. I beg you, my Lord, to be good enough to assure His Majesty of it, and that there is no obstacle I will not overcome to prevent the English from making any progress, or to make them pay very dearly for it.

I am with very deep respect, my Lord, your very humble and very obedient servant. Vaudreuil (in clear)

Letter no. 1389 — Montréal, 10 April 1759

My Lord,

I have the honour to send you herewith a copy 1. of the letter the Marquis de Montcalm wrote me on 27 February last; 2. of a memorandum giving on one side the Marquis de Montcalm's reflections and on the other my answers; 3. of the summary of the [...] of my general operations for this campaign, which I handed to the Marquis de Montcalm. You will see from all these papers, my Lord, what the Marquis de Montcalm's opinion was.

I have the honour to point out to you, for yourself alone, my Lord, that the Marquis de Montcalm's way of thinking has been public; it was the talk of officer, townsman, soldier and militiaman long before it became known to me. Unfortunately he did not voice his opinion, when he spoke it aloud and talked with all and sundry, with as much discretion as he did in his letter and his written reflections. From this followed a flood of arguments that soon went round every parish. The loss of the colony has been regarded as quite evident; the measures I take for its preservation have been criticised by certain officers of the land troops, who added the most improper remarks about me before the people themselves; and this people, already only too weary of the war, short of subsistence and of all its other most pressing needs, and feeling at the same time the goodness and vigour of its constitution weakening; this people, I say, would be easy to persuade; the evil it is threatened with frightens it and would discourage it if I did not reassure it, and if my firmness and the confidence it has in me did [not] revive its zeal and its ardour for the King's service.

I have seen only too well that all this talk {did} not displease the Marquis de Montcalm. The progress it has made is unknown to no one; but the officers who started it are only the bolder and freer in their talk. I have asked the Marquis de Montcalm to be good enough to cut all this talk at the root, failing which I could not avoid having arrested those officers who take most part in it and sending them to France to answer to you for [their] conduct. I would already have done, my Lord, all I said on this point to the Marquis de Montcalm; but in our present circumstances I restrain myself and use gentle means to bring minds round and to revive the timid; yet I shall have to take a severe course if the case requires it, to prevent a greater evil: that {is} something I shall do only {as} a last resort.

I do justice to the officers of the land troops in general, as is their {due}; many of them have a circumspection equal {to} their zeal. None of this prevents me, my Lord, from seizing every occasion to keep as much union as understanding between the Marquis de Montcalm and myself. I shall pass over in silence all he has said and may say about me; far {from} showing him any resentment, I give him marks of my confidence; in short I do everything to avoid the scandal of a break between him and me. I consider only the good of the service itself and the glory of His Majesty's arms.

I await your first despatches, my Lord, with the greatest impatience. I hope you will have been good enough to enter into the reasons I have set out to you alone. Meanwhile, so as to have nothing to reproach myself with, you see that I have told the Marquis de Montcalm that I expect him to take command of the army of Carillon.

I am with very deep respect, my Lord, your very humble and very obedient servant. Vaudreuil (in clear)

Letter no. 1390 — Montréal, 16 April 1759

My Lord,

Fearing that next year we may find ourselves in the same dearth as this one, I have urged the contractor [munitionnaire] to order his correspondents in France that, should they learn of the capture of some of the ships they have loaded with provisions for him, they replace them at once and send him new cargoes from any port whatever.

I have the honour, my Lord, to inform {you} of this arrangement and to beg you to be good enough to {have} the contractor's correspondents supplied with the ships they will need, should they be unable to find any; the contractor will pay the King in Canada the freight of these ships at this year's rate. The risks are too great for him to pay that freight at any price whatever, which obliges him to write to his correspondents that he does not mean to pay the freight anywhere but in the colony.

For the rest, my Lord, I can only repeat my wish that you add a supplement to the shipments of provisions that {will be} made to us this year; on this above all depends the preservation of the colony, and without it it would fall of {it}self.

I am with very deep respect, my Lord, your very humble and very obedient servant. Vaudreuil (in clear)

Letter no. 1391 — Montréal, 13 August 1760

My Lord,

In separate letters I have dealt with what has happened in the various parts of the colony since the last accounts I had the honour to give you. I have kept for this cipher letter particulars of which it would be dangerous for the enemy to learn at this critical moment.

You will easily have judged, my Lord, the danger run by the three ships, the stores and the troops at Restigouche under the orders of M. Danjac. {We} must indeed fear everything from the extreme superiority of the naval forces [which] hold that post and [...] the ships blockaded. M. Danjac will, I think, do his best to follow to the letter the orders I have given according to the needs of each case, but his zeal may [give way] under the perseverance and obstinacy of the enemy, who will want at any price to seize these ships, provisions and munitions. Time will tell us what [will come of it].

The only hope left me, and which I wish still more [...], [is] that M. Danjac, having received my despatches for you, my Lord, [and the] urgent orders I gave him on that occasion, will have decided to send off the frigate [the] Machault; that Sieur Lagiraudays [will have] seized a favourable moment to slip past the enemy ships by night {and} will have escaped the frigates that went in pursuit of him. The duplicates of these same despatches will reach you, my Lord, by the schooner l'Extravagante, which has been in the Baie des Chaleurs since last autumn.

M. de Villemont, to whom I had granted leave to carry the first copies to you, was detached by M. Danjac to report the situation to me. This officer, who is full of zeal, will finish {his} campaign here, and I am quite sure he will seize every occasion to distinguish himself.

We are without a navy or anything like one. The English are masters of our waters; they can go wherever they like on the river. Their fleet has now passed {Lake} Saint-François [the group for "se le" is written twice]; the passage of the [...] at the outlet of that lake cannot be obstructed; we have absolutely nothing in the colony for that. The King's flute la Marie and our feluccas [...] on this side of Saint-François [...]; so the English [will be able] to go by water to whatever place General Amherst has appointed for their junction.

The manoeuvre I ordered M. D[umas] to make {has held back} this fleet; it has [a] ship opposite it [...] this officer; and now that it is [de]cided that it does not want [...] [T]rois-Rivières, I have left M. de Longueuil in that town with a modest garrison.

However, twenty-two English [ships] have passed [...] Cartier; it is said that [...] others carrying the land[ing force] and the rest of the troops of [Lou]is[bourg]; they are said to be already at the [...] [...]. Everything shows me that the English are bent on making a diversion of [...], however weak they may be; [their] main object being to [...] towards the heart of the [colony], I am drawing M. [...] closer; I keep my forces [u]nited and ready to seize the favourable moment to give battle.

The English have begun their landing on the north shore; they behave there as on the south: they make {seductive} speeches to the Canadians; they make a marked show of paying them for the refreshments they need in salt, brandy and other essential articles of which the colony is totally bereft; they give them everything cheaper than they ever had it in {time} of peace; they gently seize the arms they have at home; they keep telling them that they alone can help them in their misery; but they warn them at the same time that the houses of the farms whose men are absent will be burnt. That is an evil, my Lord, which I cannot remedy; the English, masters of the waters, are always able to [forestall] our detachments, if they [crush] our small forces [piece]meal; all the rest would cost them nothing more.

Had I had provisions, it would have been very easy for me to gather all the Canadians of the government of Quebec; their zeal for the King's service would have made them scorn the risks and the certainty they would have had of losing their farms.

Our frontier on Lake Champlain is far from [...]; although it is our best post, the small navy we have there [can]not only not compare with the enemy's, but [we] even lack the bare necessities [to] repair it.

I am in no less unfortunate a situation on Lake Ontario: the English navy dominates there; our two corvettes can neither face nor resist their two frigates; one of our corvettes has even run aground and been damaged. We have a third on the stocks which might have enabled us to dispute the mastery of the lake, but we have not one of the articles needed to finish it and make it fit to sail.

That, my Lord, is a very exact summary of our sad position.

Hunger presses us; the Canadians have their harvest to bring in, but they cannot be taken away from [the] defence of the colony: it is about to be attacked hard on every side. The English have about forty [thousand] men; what can I [set] against that? Battalions of which the fullest is not half [...] of what it should be, militia and Indian nations. These last [notice or] tire of our extreme want; nothing [remains to them] but my care and their attachment to [us]. The smallest of the enemy's armies will be infinitely superior [to] all our forces united, far from our having a single [man] to spare beyond the number of our fight[ers]; most [...] militiamen and Indians do not [understand] the design. We have only ten [thou]sand pounds of powder in the inte[ri]or of {the} colony; it will very soon be used up if we have to use our artillery at all.

We are no better off for provisions, although the Canadians hasten to supply all they have. General Amherst, who knows our extreme distress, seizes the urgent moment of our harvests to make his mightiest efforts.

The circular letter that M. Bigot had written jointly with me to the militia captains about the delay in paying the bills of exchange would have had all the effect we wished; but you will see, my Lord, from the enclosed copy of General Murray's circular letter to most of these captains, that he left nothing unsaid to discr[edit] these [bill]s of exchange and our treasury notes entirely. To overcome all [these] obstacles the contractor has paid in his bills of exchange on France for the produce of the inhabitants who had the le[ast] [...] doubt about the [King's] money; to put them more at ease, [I] had bills of exchange offered to them on my own salary; the Intendant and the Chevalier de Lévis have followed my example with {success} [...].

Such are the critical, more than critical, circumstances to which the colony is reduced. I shall make every effort my zeal [for the] King's service can suggest to me to preserve it. I beg you, my Lord, to be [good enough to] assure His Majesty that if [I] succumb, it will be only in [the] last extremity. The Chevalier de L[évis] is animated by the same zeal [...] me; I should have the greatest hopes from our close union and perfect understanding if we were less overwhelmed.

Finally, if the English complete the conquest of the colony, they will owe it only to the exhaustion of our forces and of our last resources; for if I had only the provisions and munitions that are in danger of being taken at Restigouche, that, together with the precautions I would take besides, would put me in a position to secure a retreat where I would hold out with the troops when it was no longer possible for me to stop the enemy's progress.

I am with very deep respect, my Lord, your very humble and very obedient servant. Vaudreuil (in clear)

What the letters say

8 April 1759 (no. 1388). The famine: four ounces of bread a day, cattle and horses almost all eaten. Militia census: Quebec 6,356 men, Montréal 5,455, Trois-Rivières 1,313. The plan for 1759: hold Carillon, the Belle-Rivière (Lignery at Fort Machault, after Fort Duquesne was evacuated and blown up), Niagara (Pouchot) and La Présentation; two new corvettes on Lake Ontario. Vaudreuil sees the Duke of Cumberland’s plan revived by “General Hamerts” (Amherst). Quebec will be defended only after the battle at Carillon. He asks for battalions, munitions and above all food: he has already taken the mills’ meal and the priests’ tithes.

10 April 1759 (no. 1389), “for yourself alone”. Montcalm’s view that the colony is lost has become public; officers of the land troops speak against Vaudreuil before the people. He threatens to send the ringleaders back to France, but humours Montcalm to avoid “the scandal of a break” and gives him the command of the army of Carillon.

16 April 1759 (no. 1390). Provisions: the contractor will have his correspondents in France replace at once any supply ship taken at sea; the freight will be paid to the King in Canada. Vaudreuil asks again for extra food, “without it it would fall of itself”.

13 August 1760 (no. 1391). The ships and stores at Restigouche (M. Danjac) are in danger; Vaudreuil hopes that the frigate Machault (Sieur Lagiraudays) has broken the blockade, and that the schooner l’Extravagante will carry the duplicates. The English, “masters of our waters”, number about 40,000; Murray turns the Canadians and discredits the bills of exchange; only ten thousand pounds of powder are left. “If I succumb, it will be only in the last extremity.” With the Restigouche stores he could have secured a retreat.

What Vaudreuil did not know. On 13 August 1760 the Machault no longer existed: on 8 July 1760, at the end of the battle of the Restigouche, Lieutenant La Giraudais had her scuttled, with the Bienfaisant, so that the cargo would not be taken. Montréal capitulated on 8 September.

Sources for the context. Dictionary of Canadian Biography, vol. IV, “Rigaud de Vaudreuil de Cavagnial, Pierre de”, by W. J. Eccles (biographi.ca: born 1698, died 1778, commission of 1755, Quebec surrendered 18 September 1759, Montréal 8 September 1760); list of French naval ministers (Berryer, in office 31 October / 1 November 1758 – 13 October 1761; Wikipedia); capitulation of Niagara, 25–26 July 1759 (American Battlefield Trust); battle of the Restigouche and scuttling of the Machault on 8 July 1760 (Wikipedia; Parks Canada, Battle of the Restigouche National Historic Site; reference work: J. Beattie and B. Pothier, The Battle of the Restigouche, Parks Canada, 1977, not consulted); E. B. O’Callaghan (ed.), Documents Relative to the Colonial History of the State of New-York, vol. X, 1858, pp. 974–975, after Daniel Bourdeau’s catalogue.

Limits

  1. The letter of 13 August 1760 (no. 1391) is the weakest. On the versos (fols. 147v–151v) 94 groups are cut by the binding; the available image (about 1,125 pixels) shows only their first digit. We restore about 90 from the sense, often a syllable imposed by the next line; 20 short passages stay unresolved. Without the restored words the letter is read at 91.8%; with them, at 98.6%. Daniel Bourdeau’s rule counts certain and probable words, not restored ones: the letter is therefore read in part. A higher-resolution image would settle most of them.
  2. Unresolved words in the other letters. No. 1388: three passages (fol. 58 “j’‹équivale›”, fol. 60v “transport des ‹ap-se-e-ment›”, fol. 63v “munitions ‹ta›”); groups 64 and 59 look like encipherer’s slips. No. 1389: one group cut and illegible (fol. 68v, “du précis du ‹…› de mes opérations”).
  3. Key corrected during the reading. Twenty values of the copied table were corrected after the measurement (see the key); value 629 (“préparatif” in the table, “nous” expected once on fol. 147) is left as read.
  4. A single reader of the numbers. The groups were read by agents (Claude) on images enlarged three to four times; doubtful digits were re-read from the sense. No human check against the images has been made yet.
  5. Translations. The English and Japanese translations are working translations, close to the text.
  6. No images. The images (Library and Archives Canada copies of the ANOM originals) show no open licence: they were used for research only and are not reproduced.

Prior work: reservation

  1. Deciphered at the time, never published to our knowledge. The Navy office read the April 1759 letters: an “Abstract of despatches” of 7 June 1759 (O’Callaghan, New-York Colonial Documents, vol. X, pp. 974–975) summarises those of 10 and 16 April in a sentence or two, and our reading of no. 1390 agrees with it. No full decipherment is known. The transcripts of series C11A made for the Canadian archives (reel C-2401) skip fols. 54–76; a non-exhaustive sounding of reel C-2402 (vol. 105) found neither the cipher letter of 13 August 1760 nor a decipherment of it.
  2. Not checked — reservation. Three possible sources have not yet been consulted: (1) H.-R. Casgrain, Collection des manuscrits du maréchal de Lévis; (2) the Rapport de l’archiviste de la province de Québec (RAPQ); (3) ANOM F3 16 (Moreau de Saint-Méry collection), where an inventory lists “Vaudreuil à Berryer lui annonçant en chiffres la perte de la colonie”, probably a cipher copy of no. 1391. If one of them prints a decipherment, our contribution becomes a verification, and this card will be corrected.
  3. Elsewhere. Daniel Bourdeau’s catalogue: “open”, no decipherment found (28 October 2026); nothing on DECODE; two web searches on phrases of the plaintext found nothing.

Method, validation and credits

Method: (1) the key was not reconstructed: it is the 1757 table that Daniel Bourdeau’s catalogue pointed to as a lead; it was transcribed and frozen (SHA-256) before any measurement, with a protocol written and hashed in advance; (2) one measurement, on a held-out letter: Vaudreuil to the minister, Montréal, 8 May 1759 (ANOM C11A 104, fols. 79–83), whose copy in the Canadian archives (reel C-2401) reproduces the cipher groups with the contemporary interlinear decipherment; on 1,134 groups, letter agreement 0.972, against 0.185 at best for 200 tables with the 700 values shuffled (mean 0.096); thresholds fixed in advance: 0.85, and 0.30 above the best control. About twenty groups had been seen while identifying the table (declared); (3) reading of the four letters with the table, corrected in context (v2) without going back to the measurement; (4) word count by Daniel Bourdeau’s rule (95% of the words read for sense).

Credits. Documents: Archives nationales d’outre-mer, COL C11A 104 and 105; key: COL C11E 10 (images of Library and Archives Canada, not reproduced). Finding of the four letters and lead to the key: Daniel Bourdeau (catalogue, nos. 1388–1391), whose reading rule is applied here. Period decipherers: the Navy cipher office, author of the 1757 table, of the interlinear decipherment of the letter of 8 May 1759 used as the control, and of the June 1759 abstracts. Reading: Brice Dudout, with Claude (Anthropic), 4 November 2026. Full file (transcriptions, line-by-line decryption, key): proposal to Daniel Bourdeau.

The Leticia crisis, 1932: cipher telegrams of the Jefatura civil y militar del Amazonas

On 1 September 1932 Peruvian soldiers and civilians seized Leticia, a Colombian port on the Amazon, claiming it had been taken from the department of Loreto. Bogotá sent troops and gunboats by the Putumayo; the Colombia–Peru conflict that began then was settled only in 1934: the League of Nations administered the zone, Brazil mediated, the Rio de Janeiro protocol was signed in May 1934 and Leticia was returned to Colombia on 19 June 1934 (sources below). In the first weeks General Amadeo Rodríguez Vergara, civil and military chief of the Amazonas, at Puerto Asís, exchanged telegrams with the Ministry of War whose sensitive passages are in cipher: ammunition ordered from Bofors, gunboats, troop states, the passage of Güepí, the risk of a conflict with Ecuador on the Napo, Peruvian reinforcements in Loreto, censorship of soldiers’ mail. His papers are in the Archivo General de la Nación in Bogotá, together with the 1931 key.

The key and the first reading are Daniel Bourdeau’s. On 28 October 2026 Daniel Bourdeau found these telegrams, transcribed the key of Sección I (GARV..1.1.4, fol. 44r) and read the first telegrams (fols. 149 and 153). We re-transcribed the key independently: the table is identical to his. Our contribution: the reading of all the other alphabetic telegrams in the file, the validation of the key on a held-out telegram, the translations and the count.

Date 9–27 September 1932, in the first weeks after the seizure of Leticia (1 September 1932)
Place Bogotá ↔ Puerto Asís (Putumayo)
Senders General Amadeo Rodríguez Vergara, jefe civil y militar del Amazonas; the Ministry of War (telegrams signed Carlos Uribe Gaviria); the General Staff
Recipients the same, the other way
Source Archivo General de la Nación (Bogotá), Archivos Privados, Fondo General Amadeo Rodríguez Vergara, Asuntos militares, CO.AGN.AP.GARV..2.2.4, fols. 85–177 (DataViva); key: GARV..1.1.4, fol. 44r (rules fol. 43r) (DataViva). Images not reproduced here
Cipher seven simple-substitution alphabets, one per weekday, vowels to vowels; at the head of the telegram, in clear, the day and D (words forwards) or R (reversed). Key of Sección I of the Ministry of War, Bogotá, 31 January 1931. The clear words of a telegram stay in clear. One telegram only (No. 143, fol. 151) uses another, numeric system

Keywords Bofors · cañonero Barranquilla · Cartagena · Santa Marta · Caucayá · Güepí · Napo · Ecuador · Loreto · Manaos · vapor Nariño · clave Felixa · hidroavión · censura correspondencia

Daniel Bourdeau’s catalogue, no. 1526 ↗
Key transcribed by Daniel Bourdeau ↗
Proposal to Daniel Bourdeau (PR) ↗

State of the reading. Read in part: the alphabetic system is read by Daniel Bourdeau’s rule; the numeric telegram No. 143 is not read. Rule: 95% of words read for sense. Of the 787 cipher words of the 17 alphabetic telegrams (copies counted once): 759 certain, 24 probable {x}, none restored, 4 unresolved ‹x›; read 99.5%. Five telegrams have their period clear text in the file (fol. 117, Folio_127Recto, fols. 137, 139, 157), and fol. 141 has a pencil gloss of its last sentence: for these our reading is a verification. The other eleven have no decipherment in the file. No. 143 (fol. 151, about 160 numbers) belongs to another system, which the 1931 key does not read.

Conventions: plain word = certain (mechanical decoding gives the expected word, or a one-letter keying slip of a kind seen in the test); {x} = probable (two or more letters corrected, or a proper name not attested elsewhere); ‹x› = unresolved, given as decoded. Only the cipher words are given and counted; most clear words were not transcribed. Telegraphic style, no punctuation in the originals. In the translations, [x] = clear word supplied or evident.

Telegrams: reading (Spanish) and translation

ff. 103r–104r (Orden público 25 · 9 September 1932 · Gen. Rodríguez Vergara, Puerto Asís → Minister of War, Bogotá · heading “Viernes (D)”)

urge pedir casa {bofors} mil proyectiles {perforantes} mil {shrapnells} mil granadas para piezas artilleria cañoneros hoy solo cuentan ambos con doscientos noventa {shrapnells} doscientos noventa y seis granadas juzgo conveniente traslado cañonero barranquilla formar parte flotilla amazonas pues peruanos disponen cinco lanchas de guerra y numerosas {embarcaciones} mercantes que facilmente pueden armarse en guerra barranquilla podria conducirlo tripulacion sus ordenes adquiriendo combustible en curazao si ministerio resuelve envio cañonero barranquilla transportar municion solicitase urgentemente y piezas artilleria hallanse cartagena popa cañoneros municion debe situarse

Translation. urgent to order from the Bofors firm a thousand armour-piercing shells, a thousand shrapnel, a thousand shells for the gunboats' artillery pieces; today both have only two hundred and ninety shrapnel and two hundred and ninety-six shells; I judge it advisable to transfer the gunboat Barranquilla to form part of the Amazon flotilla, since the Peruvians have five war launches and numerous merchant vessels that can easily be armed for war; the Barranquilla could be taken by her crew under your orders, buying fuel at Curaçao; if the Ministry decides to send the gunboat Barranquilla, request transport of ammunition urgently, and the artillery pieces are at Cartagena; the gunboats' ammunition must be placed

f. 107r (= f. 106r) (No. 11487 · 10 September 1932 · Ministry of War, Bogotá → Gen. Rodríguez, Puerto Asís · heading “Sabado, d” · quotes a message from Manaos of 9 September)

manaos {zarpo} vapor nariño {tocantins} radio receptor emisor onda metros bogota oficiales respondera llamada nariño lleva toneladas aceite combustible cajas gasolina avion ‹zeffe› provisiones meses viveres {cien} {hombres} meses y botiquin medicamentos nariño clave {felixa} sistema siete leticia {hidroavion} iquitos

Translation. Manaos: the steamer Nariño {sailed} [for] {Tocantins}, radio receiver-transmitter, wavelength [...] metres, Bogotá officers will answer the call; the Nariño carries tons of fuel oil, cases of aviation petrol, [...] provisions for months, food [for] {a hundred} {men} for months and a medicine chest; the Nariño [has] the key {Felixa}, system seven; Leticia {seaplane} Iquitos

f. 109r (Orden público 83 · 18 September 1932 · Gen. Rodríguez Vergara, Puerto Asís → Minister of War, Bogotá · no day heading (Monday))

Period clear text in the file: image Folio_127Recto

precision si nos conflicto internacional ecuador paso tropas napo teniendo cuenta todas vertientes napo hasta amazonas fueron cedidas a ecuador situacion favorecenos sentido peru ocupa todas vertientes napo hasta puerto pantoja cerca bocana aguarico

Translation. precision: if we [have] an international conflict with Ecuador [by the] passage of troops [on the] Napo, bearing in mind that all the slopes of the Napo down to the Amazon were ceded to Ecuador, the situation favours us in the sense that Peru occupies all the slopes of the Napo as far as Puerto Pantoja near the mouth of the Aguarico

f. 115r (No. 777 · 14 September 1932 · Ministry of War, Bogotá → Gen. Rodríguez, Puerto Asís · heading “Miercoles, D”)

cañonero debe ponerse en marcha para inmediatamente llevando mayor numero tropas pueda transportar y toda la gasolina disponible dejando cinco cajas fecha y hora partida

Translation. the gunboat must set off for [Caucayá] immediately, carrying the largest number of troops it can transport and all the petrol available, leaving five cases; date and hour of departure

f. 116r (Orden público 57 · 14 September 1932 · Gen. Rodríguez Vergara, Puerto Asís → Minister of War, Bogotá · heading “Lunes (D)”)

Period clear text in the file: f. 117r

resto batallon boyaca hombres llegaran esta viernes tarde gasolina domingo cañonero listo zarpar apenas lleguen interesa saber si junin viene tropa guarnecer ese caso llevariame los hombres boyaca pues concepto asis quedar desguarnecido

Translation. rest of the Boyacá battalion, [160] men, will arrive here Friday afternoon, petrol Sunday; gunboat ready to sail as soon as they arrive; important to know whether Junín is sending troops to garrison; in that case I would take the Boyacá men, since in my opinion Asís [cannot] be left without a garrison

f. 125r (= f. 132r) (No. 6150 · 17 September 1932 · Ministry of War, Bogotá → Gen. Rodríguez, Puerto Asís · heading “Sabado, d”)

pasto {despachenles} cien mil cartuchos material guerra tramitelos en clave

Translation. Pasto {send them} a hundred thousand cartridges; war material: handle it in cipher

Folio_126Recto + f. 128r (Orden público 82 · 18 September 1932 · Gen. Rodríguez Vergara, Puerto Asís → Minister of War, Bogotá · heading “Lunes D.” · the piece held out for the validation (pencil foliation 127))

tropas guarnicion puerto asis jefatura personal boyaca teniente coronel jose manuel paz dos oficiales subalternos un oficial sanidad ciento sesenta y seis tropa guarnicion puerto ospina personal boyaca capitan guillermo diago tres oficiales subalternos setenta y nueve tropa guarnicion caucaya coronel roberto rico compañia colonizacion capitan carlos bejarano dos oficiales subalternos cincuenta tropa compañia construcciones capitan julio {gurin} tres oficiales subalternos noventa tropa guarnicion encanto quince tropa guarnicion florencia mayores angel m diago otoniel navas seis oficiales subalternos un oficial sanidad ciento treinta y nueve tropa potosi teniente justo guerrero flotilla guerra cañonero cartagena en puerto asis mayor jose d solano teniente hernando mora treinta tropa cañonero santa marta caucaya teniente luis a baquero oficial sanidad treinta tropa navegando en orteguaza teniente diego muñoz subtenientes artilleros flotilla jose pacheco efren salcedo resumen un general un coronel un teniente coronel tres mayores cuatro capitanes veintidos oficiales inferiores cuatro oficiales sanidad cuatrocientos noventa y nueve tropa creo situacion exige llevar leticia mayor numero tropa podria conducirse lanchas {inchiroca} ciento cincuenta hombres huayna capac ciento cincuenta cartagena cincuenta santa marta cincuenta suma cuatrocientos tendriamos disponibles cincuenta compañia colonizacion noventa compañia construcciones ciento sesenta y seis batallon boyaca suma trescientos seis desguarnecidos puerto asis caucaya puntos deben quedar con fuertes nucleos tropa traslado tropa existente florencia a caucaya y reservas boyaca a puerto asis

Translation. troops: garrison of Puerto Asís, headquarters, Boyacá personnel, Lt-Col. José Manuel Paz, two junior officers, one medical officer, one hundred and sixty-six men; garrison of Puerto Ospina, Boyacá personnel, Capt. Guillermo Diago, three junior officers, seventy-nine men; garrison of Caucayá, Col. Roberto Rico; colonisation company, Capt. Carlos Bejarano, two junior officers, fifty men; construction company, Capt. Julio {Gurin}, three junior officers, ninety men; garrison of El Encanto fifteen men; garrison of Florencia, Majors Ángel M. Diago and Otoniel Navas, six junior officers, one medical officer, one hundred and thirty-nine men; Potosí, Lt. Justo Guerrero; war flotilla: gunboat Cartagena at Puerto Asís, Major José D. Solano, Lt. Hernando Mora, thirty men; gunboat Santa Marta, Caucayá, Lt. Luis A. Baquero, medical officer, thirty men; sailing on the Orteguaza, Lt. Diego Muñoz; flotilla gunner second lieutenants José Pacheco, Efrén Salcedo; summary: one general, one colonel, one lieutenant-colonel, three majors, four captains, twenty-two junior officers, four medical officers, four hundred and ninety-nine men. I believe the situation requires taking the largest number of troops to Leticia; they could be carried by the launches {Inchiroca} one hundred and fifty men, Huayna Cápac one hundred and fifty, Cartagena fifty, Santa Marta fifty, total four hundred; we would have available fifty of the colonisation company, ninety of the construction company, one hundred and sixty-six of the Boyacá battalion, total three hundred and six, leaving Puerto Asís and Caucayá ungarrisoned, points that must keep strong bodies of troops; transfer of the troops at Florencia to Caucayá and of the Boyacá reserves to Puerto Asís

f. 130r (Orden público 89 · 19 September 1932 · Gen. Rodríguez Vergara, Puerto Asís → Minister of War, Bogotá · heading “Lunes D.”)

consulto si debo trasladarme caucaya en cañonero cartagena o permanecer esta mientras termina concentracion tropas en caso segundo ruego poner mis ordenes un hidroavion permitame facil {transporte} caucaya florencia asis fin facilitar direccion operaciones

Translation. I ask whether I should move to Caucayá in the gunboat Cartagena or stay here while the concentration of troops is completed; in the second case I beg you to put a seaplane at my orders to allow me easy {transport} Caucayá-Florencia-Asís, so as to facilitate the direction of operations

f. 134r (Orden público 110 · 20 September 1932 · Gen. Rodríguez Vergara, Puerto Asís → Minister of War, Bogotá · heading “Martes D.” · headed “Martes D.” but enciphered with the Monday alphabet)

Period clear text in the file: f. 137r

asaltantes leticia organizado defensa fortificacion emplazamiento artilleria iquitos regimiento arma cañoneras peruanas artilladas caso operaciones unicamente toma leticia defensa puertos dotar tropas confieseles tarea de una bateria provista municiones numero mayor ametralladoras solo disponemos dos piezas cañoneros escasamente municion para dos horas combate

Translation. the attackers of Leticia have organised defence, fortification, emplacement of artillery; Iquitos regiment; they arm Peruvian gunboats with artillery; in case of operations, solely the taking of Leticia [and] defence of ports, provide the troops with [the task] of a battery supplied with ammunition [and a] larger number of machine guns; we have only two pieces [on the] gunboats, with ammunition for barely two hours of combat

f. 138r (Urgente OP No. 12599 · 20 September 1932 · Carlos Uribe Gaviria, Ministry of War, Bogotá → Gen. Rodríguez · heading “Martes D”)

Period clear text in the file: f. 139r

paso tropas napo crearianos conflicto internacional ecuador servidor

Translation. [I consider it is not possible the] passage of troops [on the] Napo, [as it] would create for us an international conflict [with] Ecuador. [Your] servant [Carlos Uribe Gaviria]

f. 140r (Urgente No. 12141 · 20 September 1932 · Ministry of War, Bogotá → Gen. Rodríguez, Puerto Asís · heading “Martes, D”)

situacion leticia continua igual no tenemos noticias del encanto ni tarapaca gobierno peruano ha {decidido} todavia su actitud continuamos enviando tropas a caucaya saldra una bateria completa de bogota para caucaya general balcazar saldra y dara a usted y coronel rico mayor informacion se hace necesario que viaje cañonero hacia caucaya se haga con toda precaucion al paso de {guepi} si alli presentase resistencia hay que atacar si se cuenta con todas probabilidades exito completo las consecuencias serian funestas usted debe permanecer puerto asis para organizar {concentracion} que sera necesaria si {acontecimientos} exigenlo tan pronto sea posible enviaremos hidroavion {usted} solicita avisar salida cañonero para caucaya y numero tropas

Translation. the situation at Leticia remains the same; we have no news of El Encanto or Tarapacá; the Peruvian government has [not] yet {decided} its attitude; we continue sending troops to Caucayá; a complete battery will leave Bogotá for Caucayá; General Balcázar will leave and will give you and Colonel Rico more information; it is necessary that the gunboat's voyage to Caucayá be made with every precaution on passing {Güepí}; if resistance were offered there, attack [only] if every probability of complete success is assured [, otherwise] the consequences would be disastrous; you must stay at Puerto Asís to organise the {concentration} that will be necessary if {events} require it; as soon as possible we will send the seaplane {you} request; report the departure of the gunboat for Caucayá and the number of troops

f. 141r (No. 116 · 21 September 1932 · Gen. Rodríguez Vergara, Puerto Asís → Minister of War, Bogotá · no day heading (Monday) · corrects the end of No. 82 (“desde donde dice situación exige”))

llevar leticia mayor numero tropa podria conducirse lanchas inchiroca ciento cincuenta huayna capac ciento cincuenta cartagena cincuenta santa marta cincuenta total cuatrocientos tendriamos disponibles cincuenta compañia colonizacion noventa compañia construcciones ciento sesenta y seis batallon boyaca suma trescientos seis desguarnecidos puerto asis caucaya puntos deben quedar con fuertes nucleos tropa traslado tropa existente florencia a caucaya y reservas boyaca a puerto asis rectifico computo tropas quinientos noventa y nueve

Translation. take the largest number of troops to Leticia; they could be carried by the launches Inchiroca one hundred and fifty, Huayna Cápac one hundred and fifty, Cartagena fifty, Santa Marta fifty, total four hundred; we would have available fifty of the colonisation company, ninety of the construction company, one hundred and sixty-six of the Boyacá battalion, total three hundred and six, leaving Puerto Asís and Caucayá ungarrisoned, points that must keep strong bodies of troops; transfer of the troops at Florencia to Caucayá and of the Boyacá reserves to Puerto Asís. I correct the count of troops: five hundred and ninety-nine

f. 149r (No. 141 · 24 September 1932 · Gen. Rodríguez Vergara, Puerto Asís → Minister of War, Bogotá · heading “Lunes D.” · first read by Daniel Bourdeau (28 October 2026))

Key first transcribed by Daniel Bourdeau (28 October 2026), re-transcribed independently on 4 November 2026: identical. Each column gives the cipher letter of the day. All the telegrams seen are “D” (words forwards). Fol. 134 is headed “Martes D.” but enciphered with the Monday alphabet; fols. 109, 141 and 170 have no heading (Monday, Monday, Tuesday).

The numeric telegram No. 143 (fol. 151), not read

On 25 September 1932 Lieutenant-Colonel Paz telegraphed from Puerto Asís “Informo S.S.:”, followed by about 160 hyphenated numbers from 1 to 181. It is another, numeric system: the day key does not read it and no key for it is in hand. Lead: the Presidency key in the same collection (GARV..2.2.1, fols. 6v, 8, 10), not yet tried. This is why the whole is classed “read in part”.

Limits

  1. Many keying and transmission slips (b/h, vowels i/e/a, dropped letters); the reading normalises them. One-letter slips of a kind seen in the test count as certain; beyond that the word is probable.
  2. Four unresolved words: zeffe (fol. 107), pascama (fol. 153), hsla (fol. 159, to be re-read at full resolution), gixhtlo (fol. 170). On fol. 153 the passage around “relator … yo” does not construe: relator and yo decode cleanly, but their sense is not established.
  3. Clear words not transcribed. Most clear words of the telegrams were not recorded: the reading gives the cipher parts, and the translations supply evident clear words in brackets.
  4. A single reader (Claude agents), on the DataViva images; no human check against the images so far.
  5. No images. The DataViva records show no explicit licence: the images were used for research only.

Prior work

  1. Daniel Bourdeau: finding, key and first readings (fols. 149 and 153), 28 October 2026; catalogue verdict “open”.
  2. Period clear texts in the file: fol. 117r (No. 57), image Folio_127Recto (No. 83), fol. 137r (“CIFRADO N° 110”), fol. 139r (No. 12599), fol. 157r (“CIFRADO No. 12.441”); pencil gloss on fol. 141r. Fol. 123r (“URGENTE CIFRADO N° 11.831”) is a clear text whose cipher is not in the file.
  3. Publications: no edition or study of these telegrams found (catalogue searches, 3 November 2026: DECODE, Cryptiana, Lasry, FRUS 1932 vol. V, web). The historiography of the Colombia–Peru war has not been searched: this is a reservation.
  4. Sources for the context: seizure of Leticia on 1 September 1932 and return on 19 June 1934 (Encyclopedia of Latin American History and Culture, “Leticia Dispute”); the Loreto claim and the “Pacto de Río” of May 1934 (J. C. Vargas, “El conflicto de Leticia: un capítulo desconocido”, Nova et Vetera, Universidad del Rosario, 9 November 2021, online); Rio Protocol, 24 May 1934 (Wikipedia). Facts about the Jefatura, Puerto Asís and the telegrams come from the file itself.

Method, validation and credits

Method: (1) key re-transcribed from the image and compared with Daniel Bourdeau’s (identical), then frozen; protocol written and hashed (SHA-256) before any computation; (2) one measurement on a held-out telegram, No. 82 (image Folio_126Recto, 661 cipher letters, 103 words), compared with an independent reading of the same image frozen before decoding: 0.977 character agreement and 0.854 word agreement, against 0.381 and 0.039 at best for 200 shuffled keys (vowels to vowels, consonants to consonants); thresholds fixed in advance: 0.85, and 0.30 above the best control; (3) reading of every alphabetic telegram in the file with the key unchanged; each probable or unresolved word was re-decoded and regraded; (4) check against the five period clear texts.

Credits. Daniel Bourdeau: finding (catalogue, no. 1526), transcription of the key and first reading of fols. 149 and 153; reading rule. Period decipherers: the services of the Ministry of War and of the Jefatura, authors of the 1931 key and of the clear texts kept in the file. Documents: Archivo General de la Nación, Bogotá (DataViva images, not reproduced). Reading of the other telegrams, validation and translations: Brice Dudout, with Claude (Anthropic), 4 November 2026. Full file: proposal to Daniel Bourdeau.

Alfonso II del Carretto, Marquis of Finale, to his agents in Milan, Regensburg, 2 September 1576

By 1576 Alfonso II del Carretto had lost his marquisate of Finale: driven out by a revolt of his subjects, he saw the imperial fief run since 1566 by the emperor’s commissioners, while Genoa and Philip II’s Spain coveted it. A prince of the Empire since 1564, he followed the imperial court to the Diet of Regensburg and on 2 September wrote to his two agents in Milan, Lodovico Allaria and Paolo Fenocchio. The top of the letter, eleven lines, is in cipher: it concerns a man recommended to “His Majesty”, Count Spinola (“Espinula”) and one Beccaria. There is no contemporary decipherment on the document. We give its first reading, with a key recovered from the ciphertext alone.

Date Regensburg, 2 September 1576 (Imperial Diet)
Place Regensburg → Milan
Sender Alfonso II del Carretto, Marquis of Finale, signing “il principe marchese del Final”
Recipients Lodovico Allaria and Paolo Fenocchio, his agents in Milan (address on the verso: “Alli Nobili Agenti nri car.mi … Milano”)
Source Modena, Biblioteca Estense Universitaria, Autografoteca Campori, Lettera D, Del Carretto, Alfonso II (sec. XVI), c. 10; digitised by the Lodovico Media Library (no image reproduced here: no licence stated)
Cipher substitution of Italian with homophones for the vowels (a, e, o, i, u have two to four signs each), Latin letters, Greek-like signs and digits for the consonants, word division kept; an isolated o is a null; no nomenclator. Key reconstructed here (table below)

Keywords Beccaria · il conte Espinula · ordini di sua maiestà · il signor Pietro · la qualità del huomo · persona di fe · li suoi ministri · l’intento

Entry in Daniel Bourdeau’s catalogue ↗
Daniel Bourdeau’s repository ↗

State of the reading. Read; unpublished to our knowledge (prior work re-checked on 9 November 2026, see Limits). Rule applied: Daniel Bourdeau’s, 95% of words read for sense, restored words not counted. Of the 182 cipher words: 149 certain, 25 probable {x}, 2 restored [x], 6 unresolved ‹…›; words read (certain and probable): 174 / 182 = 95.6% (96.7% with the restored ones). The 6 unresolved words are all in the torn left margin; the cipher block itself is read in full. Key validated by a single measurement on three held-out lines (0.961 against at best 0.263 for 200 controls).

Conventions: plain word = certain (every letter given by the key); {x} = probable (one sign departs from the key, settled by the sense); [x] = restored from the sense; ‹…› = unresolved; letters in brackets inside a word ({giudi[ce]}) are cut off at the edge of the leaf. Spelling of the letter (ponto, soa, essequire, huomo); accents and apostrophes added. One line = one cipher line; M1–M5 = notes in the torn margin. The count follows the cipher groups: “il conte” and “l’intento” are each written as one group and count as one word.

Established text

L01 il Beccaria ha fra le altre cose detto che non è persona che

L02 possa {meglio} né così bene come il conte Espinula essequire li ordini di sua {maiestà}

L03 et {ci} assicura non mancherà di essequire {mentre} sia solo da questo solo {poi} far {giudi[ce]}

L04 il signor Pietro del resto et della qualità del huomo ma sia pur certo che non {habbian} {manca[to]}

L05 né siamo per mancar ponto di {far} {conoscere} il vero così in honore di soa signoria come in

L06 servitio di {sua} maiestà et {nostro} ancora benché ne {apporti} qualche {difficultà} l’esser

L07 costui {approuato} della maniere da sua signoria havendolo come persona di fe

L08 destinato a sua maiestà et come che si sia più tosto diportato bene che male [però]

L09 stia pur sua signoria et attenda a far il {debito} da quella parte si come {habbian}

L10 fatto et faremo noi da questa che sendo costui conosciuto da {sua} maiestà et {dalli} [suoi] {ministri}

L11 più che {lui} forse non si crede si promettiamo che né lui né quello {per} {cui} egli {procura} {hauranno} l’intento

Sign names of our transcription: z = ʒ, P/p = ρ, Q = barred q, 1, 2, 3 = the groups oρo, oρ and oρ· read as single signs; ρ followed by a heavy dot is u, plain ρ is l. Key published under CC BY 4.0 in Daniel Bourdeau’s repository (key.tsv).

Summary of the sense

Spinola. Beccaria has said, among other things, that no one could carry out His Majesty’s orders better or as well as Count “Espinula” (Spinola, in its Spanish form), and he assures that he will not fail to carry them out, provided they are left to him alone; let Signor Pietro then judge the rest and the quality of the man.

The recommended man. The marquis has not failed and will not fail in any point to make the truth known, for his correspondent’s honour as for His Majesty’s service and his own; the difficulty is that this man was approved and sent to His Majesty as a trustworthy person, and that he has behaved rather well than badly.

Instruction. Let the agents rest easy and do their duty on their side, as the marquis has done and will do on his: the man is better known to His Majesty and his ministers than is believed, and neither he nor the one he acts for will reach their aim.

To be identified. “His Majesty” is probably Philip II (or the emperor, the letter being written at the Diet); Beccaria, Signor Pietro and the man himself are not identified. The background is the Finale dispute between the marquis, his subjects, Genoa, Spain and the Empire.

Doubtful and unresolved words, limits

  1. The 25 probable words (finishing). Each departs from the key by one sign only, and the sense settles it with no other plausible choice: {meglio} (key gives “maglio”, D/G confused), {maiestà} (“maidsta”, ʒ/ɔ alike), {ci} (“cce”: “et ci assicura”), {mentre} (n doubled), {poi} (“poo”), {giudi[ce]} and {manca[to]} (words at the edge of the leaf, end cut or abbreviated), {habbian} ×2 (“harbbian”, one r too many, same spelling twice: the encipherer’s habit), {far} (s for f, letters alike even in clear), {conoscere} (ρ for e), {sua} ×2 (isolated o = null), {nostro} (ɔ for t), {apporti} and {approuato} (second sign doubled), {difficultà} (first sign of a different shape, = d by the sense and by dd = ff), {debito} (r for b), {dalli} (word division), {ministri} (“ri” interlinear, t left out), {lui}, {cui}, {hauranno} (ρo for u, the dot of ρ lost?), {per} (a for e), {procura} (g for u). Several are probably slips of our single-pass transcription: no blind re-reading of the doubtful signs has been done.
  2. The 2 restored words. [però] (L08): the word is at the torn edge, the key gives “perel”; “però stia pur…” follows from the sense. [suoi] (L10): one sign (é) occurs nowhere else; the o is given by the sense (“dalli suoi ministri”).
  3. The 6 unresolved words. All in the torn left margin (M1–M5): only word ends survive (“…etche”, “…eotto”, “…asserano”, “…o”) and “loo”, “ene” (bene?). Only the original could restore them, if anything is left.
  4. No contemporary clear. The key is validated against an independent automatic break of the held-out lines, not against a clear text of the time. The transcription is a single pass without a second reader; the clear part of the letter is not transcribed here.
  5. Prior work (re-checked on 9 November 2026). No decipherment on the document or on the neighbouring letter (c. 9, Vienna 1574, in clear); entry no. 2164 of Daniel Bourdeau’s catalogue notes none; no target or lead on this text in his repository before our PR. Two searches on 4 November and two more on 9 November found no edition. Not checked: A. G. Cavagna, La biblioteca di Alfonso II Del Carretto (2012), F. Edelmayer (1988) on the Finale dispute, and the agents’ papers in Genoa or Milan: a clear copy there cannot be ruled out.

Method, validation and credits

Method: (1) protocol written and hashed (SHA-256) before any calculation, with lines L09–L11 (54 words) held out; (2) shapes transcribed without any value, then frozen; (3) key broken on L01–L08 alone by simulated annealing (4-gram model of 16th-century Italian built from other texts; six seeds out of six identical), with a single correction from the sense (d = f), then frozen; (4) independent reference: a fully automatic break of L09–L11 alone, frozen before they were decoded with the key; (5) a single measurement: character agreement 0.961 against at best 0.263 for 200 shuffled keys (thresholds fixed in advance: ≥ 0.85 and ≥ control + 0.30): key validated; word agreement 0.852 (not decisive); (6) reading of the whole piece by Daniel’s rule. Declared reservation: while justifying the division of the oρ / oρo groups, one word of the held-out lines (“quella”) was seen before the measurement.

Credits. Document: Biblioteca Estense Universitaria, Modena, Autografoteca Campori (no image reproduced). Catalogue and reading rule: Daniel Bourdeau (entry no. 2164, cyphersolver, PR no. 291). Reading: Brice Dudout, with Claude (Anthropic), 4–6 November 2026.

George I Rákóczi’s conditions for the Swedish alliance, [1631–1632], fols. 491v–492v — partial reading with WAINUT’s key

This document is first of all WAINUT’s work: he found it among Ludwig Camerarius’s papers, rebuilt the key and read the first page (fol. 491r) in his target rakoczi1632 in Daniel Bourdeau’s repository (3 November 2026). With his key we read the next three pages, which he had not done (fols. 491v–492v), and put the key to a first test on a whole held-out page. The text continues the conditions set by the Prince of Transylvania for joining the alliance of the King of Sweden and the Protestant princes: money, troops, guarantees after the peace. The cipher is embedded in clear Latin, and Camerarius wrote his solution above almost every cipher word: this is transcription and verification work, not a break. On the microfilm every line ends in the binding fold, so many word endings are missing.

Date undated; 1631–1632 from the content (the King of Sweden is alive: before Lützen, 16 November 1632)
Place Transylvania → Germany (“Ragocii mandata in Germaniam missa”, Halm’s catalogue, 1874)
Author George I Rákóczi, Prince of Transylvania (copy among Ludwig Camerarius’s papers)
Recipient his envoy to the King of Sweden and the confederate princes
Source Munich, Bayerische Staatsbibliothek, Clm 10401, no. 139 (Collectio Camerariana 51), fols. 491v–492v; digitised microfilm MDZ bsb00117497, views 1200–1202 (no image reproduced here)
Cipher homophonic substitution: each Latin letter is a number from 1 to 99 (two to nine numbers per letter), separated by dots, plus about ten signs and a few three-digit groups for names (217.11.99 and 218.88 = the King of Sweden); the cipher words sit inside clear Latin. Camerarius’s interlinear glosses. Key: WAINUT’s (key_frozen.tsv, 72 entries)

Keywords Unio · Confoederati · quinquies centena millia florenorum · XVI mille pedites Germanos · IV mille cataphractos · bis mille musquetarios · Regnum Hungariae · Rex Poloniae · hibernum tempus

Key

The key is WAINUT’s (targets/rakoczi1632/key_frozen.tsv), taken with none of its values changed. Before the measurement a script added 8 values drawn from the glossed pairs of fols. 491v and 492r (on those pairs WAINUT’s key alone already agrees with the glosses on 97.0% of the 365 letters):

Signs seen with several values: {s} = l / c / o; {a} = i / u / c / g; {x} = s / f; {c} = a / b / g; 68 = b / g; 45 = h (gloss) against c (WAINUT’s key). Most “probable” words come from these.

Summary of the sense

Defence and peace. The allies will defend with all their strength the prince’s estates, inheritances and succession against any attacker, and will make peace with no one to his harm.

Money (art. 2). As long as the war lasts they will pay him every year 500,000 florins (“quinquies centena millia florenorum”) in two instalments; in the first year the sum is to be paid in one go and put into his hands before he takes the field.

Troops (arts. 3–4). During the war they will keep for him 16,000 picked German foot and 4,000 cuirassiers, all of whose officers will depend on him and be bound to him by oath with their men. Article 4 concerns the Kingdom of Hungary: whatever is ceded to him, by common arms or otherwise, they will never claim.

After the peace (arts. V–VII). If, once the war is over, enemies rise against him or his heirs, they must help him; even in peacetime, on serious suspicion of secret plots, they will keep at their own cost 2,000 musketeers and 2,000 cuirassiers and hand their pay to him. All members of the Union are to be bound by these four points.

Entering Hungary (arts. VIII–X). Before he enters Hungary they will send 16,000 foot and 4,000 cuirassiers, so that he can forestall the moves of the King of Poland in his rear; they will send him a trusted man without delay; if he is to campaign in winter with the Hungarian army, the sum asked for is to be paid to him; and both sides will act by mutual agreement, so that neither has to wait for the other.

Doubtful words, restorations and limits

  1. The fold. The volume was microfilmed bound: every line of 491v and 492v ends in the binding. Nearly all 66 restored words come from there; they are restored from Camerarius’s gloss (often legible above the fold) or, failing that, from the sense, and are never counted as read. A colour scan or the original would settle most of them.
  2. Restorations from the sense, justified. [Hungariae ?] (art. 4): the fold cuts the word after “Regno”; article VIII speaks of the “fines Hungariae”, and Rákóczi’s aim is Royal Hungary. [id ?] (art. VII): “Ad … quae IV puncta” calls for a short demonstrative. [invadent] (art. VIII): this is the gloss; the cipher gives “inten…”, so the word is also counted among the unresolved. praetendent (art. 4): the cipher’s form; the gloss has “protendent”; we keep the cipher’s spelling. [et subveni]re (art. V): two words restored from the gloss.
  3. Probable words. 47 words with at least one letter from a two-valued group — (b/t), (c/l), (d/o), (d/i) — or a many-valued sign ({s}, {a}, {x}, {c}): the gloss and the sense decide, the key alone does not. The doubtful groups 32/82, 50/80, 66/86, 56/66 have not been re-read blind.
  4. Unresolved words. 14 words, nearly all on 492v: 391.11…, 82.38 and “inten…” (gloss: invadent), “…ret”, {w}, “cur…is”, {x}.69.22, the end of one line, “…t”, 76.… The bottom lines of 492v have no gloss: they are read with the key alone, and a clear paraphrase in the left margin (“mutuo consensu et correspondentia … ne diutius alterutrum … praestolari”) bears them out.
  5. Count. The split into certain / probable / restored / unresolved is a single-pass manual count (6 November 2026), not checked independently. Mechanical check on 9 November on the text published here: 66 words carry brackets and 6 are wholly lost ([…]); so at most 237 − 72 = 165 cipher words lie outside brackets, at most 69.6%; the rate used, 66.2%, is the stricter one. Transcription made in a single pass by an AI agent on the microfilm, without a palaeographer; review grade “B” (read in part).
  6. Prior work (re-checked on 9 November 2026). Camerarius’s glosses are the contemporary decipherment. WAINUT searched for a printed text (Szilágyi, 1873 and 1882, including the Okirattár of Paul Strassburg’s mission of 1631–1633) without finding one; we have not redone that search line by line. Today his target rakoczi1632 is unchanged since 4 November (last commit 4e0b8af13) and still gives fols. 491v–492v as “not done” beyond his 12 control words; a quick web search finds neither an edition of these conditions nor a reading of the cipher. An edition of the conditions in clear, from another copy, cannot be ruled out.

Method, validation and credits

Method: (1) protocol written and hashed (SHA-256 8bb97f93…) before any transcription of fols. 491v–492v, fixing in advance the held-out page (all the cipher of 492v), the measure and the thresholds (agreement ≥ 0.85 and margin ≥ 0.30 over the best of 200 controls); (2) 492v transcribed on strips with the glosses masked, then frozen; (3) key K = WAINUT’s key + 8 values drawn by script from the glosses of 491v–492r, frozen; (4) glosses of 492v read only then; (5) a single measurement: on 31 glossed words (205 letters), agreement 0.902 between the decipherment with K and the gloss, against at best 0.341 for 200 shuffled keys (margin 0.561): key validated. WAINUT’s key alone gives 0.878 (margin 0.571). This is the first test of his key outside fol. 491r beyond his 12 control words. Incident disclosed: one masked strip (y565) was a gloss line; the next line was left out of the measurement, as were two words of which a fragment of gloss had been seen.

Credits. WAINUT: the document, the key, the reading of fol. 491r and the prior-art search, on which all of this rests (target rakoczi1632). Contemporary decipherment: Ludwig Camerarius’s glosses. Document: Bayerische Staatsbibliothek, Clm 10401, no. 139, MDZ digitised microfilm. Reading rule and catalogue: Daniel Bourdeau (cyphersolver). Transcription and reading of fols. 491v–492v, test of the key: Brice Dudout, with Claude (Anthropic), 6 November 2026 (PR #297).

Letter of “Dahka” from Cracow, 1715 — partial reading

A Polish letter signed “Dahka” (Daniel Bourdeau’s catalogue writes “Dahku”), sent from Cracow in 1715 and kept among the papers of Anna Branicka née Potocka in the Central Archives of Historical Records in Warsaw (AGAD). The letter is in clear, except for a passage of seventeen lines written in graphic signs, with a few Polish words in clear among them. No key, gloss or deciphered copy comes with it. We broke the cipher on the ciphertext alone: it is a letter-for-letter substitution of Polish. The passage reports a move by the deputies of the Sandomierz voivodeship in the autumn of 1715, on the eve of the Confederation of Tarnogród against the Saxon troops of Augustus II. We publish the reading as far as we could take it, gaps included: 84.1% of the cipher words, with a key that our own protocol validates only in part.

Date Cracow, 1715; the unit card gives “1715, IX, 21”, and the cipher speaks of 9 October as still to come: probably 21 September 1715 (the date line of p. 1 was not re-read; our first sorting note said 21 May, probably wrongly)
Place Cracow → recipient not identified
Sender signed “Dahka” (catalogue: “Dahku”); not identified
Recipient not identified (address in clear, not transcribed here)
Source Warsaw, Archiwum Główne Akt Dawnych, fonds 338 (Zbiór Anny z Potockich Branickiej), 1/338/0/1/682, scan 3 (pp. 2–3); szukajwarchiwach, unit 28224391; Bourdeau catalogue no. 1581 (“Część listu pisana szyfrem, nierozwiązanym”)
Cipher letter-for-letter substitution of Polish with 24 graphic signs for 20 letters and a few homophones (a = + / P, z = W / N, y = z / l, w = b / C); a framed sign (N, twice) and a tied sign (C, once) stand where names are expected: probably a small nomenclator. Word breaks as in the manuscript. Key reconstructed here (table below)

Keywords posłowie sendomirscy · woisko koronne · pospolite ruszenie · pro die nona Octobris · Sendomirz · prymas · za Wisłę

State of the reading. Partial reading, explained; unpublished to our knowledge (prior work re-checked on 9 November 2026). Rule applied: Daniel Bourdeau’s, 95% of words read for sense to publish a decipherment; on this site “read” = certain + probable, restored words apart. Here, of the 63 cipher words: 39 certain, 14 probable {x}, 0 restored, 10 unresolved ‹…›; words read: 53 / 63 = 84.1% (84.1% with restored words; there are none). The threshold is not reached: this is not a complete decipherment. The key is validated only in part by our protocol: on the four held-out lines, 0.444 against at best 0.083 for 200 shuffled keys; the required margin (+0.30) is met, the absolute threshold fixed in advance (0.60) is not.

Conventions: plain word = certain (every letter given by the key); {x} = probable (one or two signs off, or a letter the key does not give, settled by the sense); [x] = letter restored inside a word written in clear (not counted); ‹…› = unresolved (the decryption as it stands, or the name of the sign); « … » = word written in clear in the letter, not counted. Spelling of the cipher and of the letter, without diacritics in the cipher; one manuscript line per line.

Translation (approximate)

… at His Grace’s of Cracow (W.D.): the Sandomierz deputies ‹…› ‹…› {in} ‹…›, [asked] that ‹N› would support with the Crown army {the levée en masse} {of the voivodeship} {of Sandomierz}, set for the ninth day of October, and that the Crown army {not be moved away} from Sandomierz. To this they received the answer that ‹N› cannot commit himself {to assistance} with the army, because one must first know what {resolution} ‹C› the Primate will give them, the Sandomierz deputies. To the deputies sent home he {declared} that the army would however not be moved away, only taken {across the Vistula} from ‹…›, straight ‹…› ‹…› side ‹…›, to declare to those at home (?).
