Signs are named by an arbitrary ASCII letter or digit, one per shape (no image: AGAD document). Raw key of the best annealing run on the training lines, frozen before the measurement. * V = g in the frozen key; after the measurement a blind shape plate showed that at d05 and e05 this sign has the shape of W: the reading uses z there (reading only; frozen key and measurement unchanged). † N (framed) and C (tied) give z and w but stand in place of names: counted unresolved.

Summary of the sense

The request. The deputies (posłowie) of Sandomierz asked that a person written with the framed sign ‹N› — no doubt a senior commander, perhaps the hetman — support with the Crown army the levée en masse of the Sandomierz voivodeship, set for 9 October, and that the army not be moved away from Sandomierz.

The answer. ‹N› cannot promise anything before knowing the Primate’s resolution (in 1715, Stanisław Szembek) to the deputies. He only declared that the army would not be withdrawn but taken across the Vistula from an unidentified place (‹kodzarzyc›).

Context (to be checked by a historian): in the autumn of 1715 the Polish nobility rose against the Saxon troops of Augustus II; the general confederation was formed at Tarnogród in November 1715. The letter shows a voivodeship arming itself and seeking the support of the Crown army, which holds back.

Probable and unresolved words, limits

  1. Partial key. The key was broken on the ciphertext alone, with no crib and no clear copy; it is validated only in part (0.444 < 0.60). The four held-out lines are used up: another letter in the same signs would be needed to test it again. The score is a lexicon score, not an agreement with a known clear text.
  2. Unresolved (10 words). Seven runs that the key gives without a recognisable word: ‹zto›, ‹e›, ‹kostalacio› (d02, perhaps a verb of asking: the sense wants “asked”); ‹kodzarzyc› (e05, a place name is expected after “przeprawić z”); ‹nadra›, ‹zo›, ‹a› (e05–e06: perhaps “na drugą stronę”, “to the other side”, but the letters do not give it; the isolated ‹a› is probably the clear word “to”, noticed after the measurement, not corrected). Three name signs: ‹N› twice (d03, d09: the subject of “chciał assistere” and of “deklarować nie może”) and ‹C› once (e01: a title or name before “prymas”).
  3. Restoration. No cipher word is restored. One letter only is added, inside a word written in clear (“posł[a]nym”, e03), not counted.
  4. Reading of the signs. A single reader (an agent) transcribed the signs, with a table of shapes fixed before the transcription; the last word of e05 is read on a reduced view, at the page edge. A blind re-reading plate (3 questions, one a control, answered by Brice Dudout on 5 November 2026) settled the barred sign V at d05 and e05; it does not change the share read (d05 moves from certain to probable, e05 stays unresolved). Counted without splitting z + noun or nie + verb, the same text gives 49 of 59 words (83%).
  5. Outside the reading. The clear parts (p. 1, address, end) are not transcribed; neither the sender, nor the recipient, nor the person behind ‹N› is identified.
  6. Prior work (re-checked on 9 November 2026). No folder or reading in Daniel Bourdeau’s repository before our target (the document was listed as “unsolved”); nothing on DECODE, from Tomokiyo or Lasry; web searches (Dahka / Dahku, Cracow 1715, Branicki papers, Sandomierz deputies and the levée of 9 October 1715) found no edition of this passage. The key “Pour déchiffrer” of the same fonds (1/338/0/1/1196) is a French numeric nomenclator, unrelated to this sign cipher.

The fourteen probable words

  • {w} (d02): a single letter between two unresolved runs; the key gives w, but the construction is not sure.
  • {pospolitego} {ruszenia} (d04): the cipher gives “pospoltema raszenia”; the sense (levée en masse, pospolite ruszenie) is certain, two or three signs are off.
  • {wdztwa} {sendomirskiego} (d05): the cipher gives “wdtwa sendomirskiezo” (with V = z, see plate V); abbreviation of województwa, ending -ego expected; one sign is off.
  • {nie} {oddalać} (d07): the cipher gives “nieoddala” as one word, without the ending; the same verb is spelt “nieoddaliac” at e03.
  • {w} {assistencyi} (d10): the cipher gives “wassistecy”; one n is missing.
  • {rezolucyą} (e01): the cipher gives “resoliacio”; the Latin-Polish word rezolucja is expected (“what resolution the Primate will give”).
  • {im} (e01): two letters given by the key; its place in the sentence is uncertain next to the tied sign ‹C›.
  • {deklarował} (e03–e04): the cipher gives “da klarowal” (a for e); the clear word “deklarować” occurs twice in the letter.
  • {za} {Wisłę} (e04): the cipher gives “zawislen” as one word; “przeprawić za Wisłę” (to take across the Vistula) follows the sense.

Method, validation and credits

Method: (1) table of shapes fixed before transcription, then the 17 lines (350 signs, 24 shapes) transcribed and frozen by SHA-256; (2) pre-registration written before any attack: the last four lines (e03–e06, 72 signs, 14 words) held out; clear words serve only as word breaks, never as known plaintext; (3) attack on the 278 training signs (d01–e02) by simulated annealing (8 restarts × 40,000 steps, at most two signs per letter) with a 4-gram model learnt from Polish clear texts of the period (Deboli’s despatches): all eight restarts give the same Polish text; raw key frozen; (4) a single measurement: share of the held-out signs covered by Polish words of five letters or more, 0.444 against at best 0.083 for 200 shuffled keys (median 0.000), margin 0.361. Thresholds fixed in advance: validated if ≥ 0.60 and ≥ controls + 0.30; partial if only the margin is met. Verdict: partial. The held-out lines read: “woisko zas nieoddaliac da klarowal | zawislen prze prawic…”; (5) reading of the whole passage by Daniel’s rule; plate V after the measurement, for the reading only.

Credits. Document: Archiwum Główne Akt Dawnych, Warsaw, fonds 338, 1/338/0/1/682 (no image reproduced). Catalogue and reading rule: Daniel Bourdeau (target dahku1715, no. 1581; cyphersolver). Key (CC BY 4.0) and reading: Brice Dudout, with Claude (Anthropic), 5–6 November 2026; shape re-reading (plate V): Brice Dudout.

Deboli and Gołuchowski, St Petersburg, cipher despatches of 1787 — partial reading

Antoni Augustyn Deboli, the Polish resident in St Petersburg, wrote to King Stanisław August in cipher; his secretary Gołuchowski also wrote, in the same code, to one of the King’s ministers. The AGAD volume that gathers the ciphers of 1787 (Zbiór Popielów, sygn. 3) has no decipherment in the margins. We sorted its pieces by system, found the key of the “older code” (the “Cyfra polska” of 8 March 1783, ZbPop 444) and read with it the fourteen pieces written in that code: the Russian regiments in Poland, Catherine II’s journey to the Crimea, the Russo-Turkish war as it begins, the alliance Warsaw hoped for. No piece reaches 95%: we publish the reading as it stands, 81.7% of the words, with the unresolved syllables left in place.

Dates 29 December 1786 – 16 October 1787 (11 despatches of Deboli, 3 letters of Gołuchowski)
Place St Petersburg → Warsaw
Senders Antoni Augustyn Deboli (1747–1810), Polish resident; Gołuchowski, his secretary
Recipients King Stanisław August; for Gołuchowski, “one of the ministers” of the King (inventory)
Source Warsaw, Archiwum Główne Akt Dawnych, Zbiór Popielów (zesp. 12), sygn. 3, “Deboli. 1787 (cyfry)”, 83 pieces, k. 184; Bourdeau catalogue no. 416
Cipher one-part Polish code in shuffled letter blocks: groups 1 to 1969 (syllables, words, names), signal group 2345, nulls from 1970. Key of the time: AGAD ZbPop 444, “Cyfra polska”, 8 March 1783, transcribed by us (1,965 entries). Other pieces of the volume are in three tables with no known key (3865, 9933, 12282) and one is in the code of 1789–1791: they are not read

Keywords regiment · Ostermann · Potemkin · Kijów · Cherson · Kobentzel · Xiąże de Ligne · Ségur · Markow · Stackelberg · Oczaków · Rumiancow

State of the reading. Partial reading, explained. Rule applied: Daniel Bourdeau’s, 95% of words read for sense to publish a decipherment; on this site “read” = certain + probable, restored words apart. Of the 7,040 words of the fourteen pieces: 5,499 certain, 256 probable {x}, 4 restored [x], 1,281 unresolved ‹…›; words read: 5,755 / 7,040 = 81.7% (81.8% with the restored ones); by piece, from 69.6% to 90.5%. No piece reaches the threshold: this is not a complete decipherment. Status of the key: the key is not rebuilt by us, it is the King’s cabinet’s own; but our test, fixed in advance, failed: on three despatches of 1788 in the same code, compared with their clears of the time, it reads 0.874, 0.874 and 0.837 on the held-out piece, against a threshold of 0.90 (shuffled-key controls: 0.12 at most). This confirms that 444 is the code of 1783–1788, far above chance, but not that it is enough to read word by word: some groups are misread on the despatches, and some values of 444 do not fit.

Conventions: plain word = certain; {x} = probable; [x] = restored from the sense; ‹…› = unresolved: syllables the key gives that make no sense in place, or a group number whose value is torn or rubbed out in the key (1215, 1216, 1398, 1405); ‹·› = group without value. Spelling of the time, as the code gives it; punctuation and word division restored. Only the cipher parts are given.

Key

Key ZbPop 444 has 1,965 entries, transcribed from its nine images (98% legible) and frozen (SHA-256) before any reading; 21 doubtful values were re-read on the image of the key alone, none was changed from the sense of a despatch. Examples: 8 = mi, 158 = nie, 803 = W. Kr. Mć (Your Majesty), 1332 = do; groups with a half mark (136½ = Nas, 157½ = nic, 192½ = nigdzie) are written “136” + “1/2”. It is not the code of 1789–1791 read by Daniel Bourdeau (where 8 = “do”). The full table is published in Daniel’s repository (folder deboli1787, key/zbpop444_v3.tsv).

Summary of the sense

1 (29 December 1786 (received 9 January 1787)). Deboli tells the King that the Vice-Chancellor's (Ostermann's) evasive answer about the Russian regiments stationed in Poland kept him from asking formally, for fear of an explicit refusal; he considers an approach through Potemkin and mentions abuses committed by the regiments. Last Wednesday he pressed the Vice-Chancellor, who said neither yes nor no, so the silence has to be read. Since the King's despatch of the 16th, he sees that Russia is not disposed to withdraw the regiments. At the next conference he will use the Department's despatch of the 9th and the argument that the Emperor, travelling to Kiev, will see Russian regiments in Poland with his own eyes. Partly read passages: Buchholtz (the Prussian envoy) spreading a "falsehood"; a visitor explaining his interests; a count's memorial on estates of Polish families in Ukraine. To the Department he writes only pro forma.

4 (9 January 1787). Deboli expects an answer at tomorrow's conference on the King's letter of the 16th (Dec.). The aim is finally to be rid of the regiment in question (cf. piece 1). The Empress's departure remains as announced. By the last Vienna courier, Joseph II will come to Kherson rather than Kiev and cannot stay long because the Neapolitan sovereigns are expected in Vienna. Potemkin will go to Krichev (his estate) to receive the Empress and will wait for her at Kiev; otherwise he could not finish his tours. The affair of the Princess of Württemberg (Augusta of Brunswick) troubles the grand-ducal couple: there was talk of sending her to Reval during the Empress's absence pending an answer from her father the Duke of Brunswick, who reportedly wrote urging her to win her husband's affection and declines to take her side or recall her; since yesterday it is said the Empress will take her along. A general, taken seriously ill on Saturday, is better. Deboli received the King's letter of 7 December yesterday.

7 (18 January 1787). Deboli reports a talk with Vice-Chancellor Ostermann about the Russian regiment stationed in Poland. Deboli presses for its withdrawal, as the Sejm instructed him. Ostermann answers that the Poles complain now of the Emperor, now of the King of Prussia, while also demanding the withdrawal. He adds that the regiment keeps the peace and that the Hetman himself complained of it. He blames Deboli's vehemence and tells him to put these points to the King. Deboli notes that he has waited for an answer for almost a year. For three years, he says, he has answered foreign envoys vaguely. The French minister, speaking to the Dutch one, assumed the King would raise the matter when he met the Empress. In Deboli's view everything depends on Potemkin, who wants the affair sent to a Commission. Deboli fears such a Commission: the grievances (Igelström, a detachment entering a district in 1783) would be turned back against Poland. He suggests the King write to Potemkin before Kiev. He will not use the King's letter of the 3rd. He also mentions Potemkin's plan to buy an estate in Poland ("S mila", probably Smiła). The letter then covers: - the affair of the Palatine of Ruthenia, with Chernyshev, General Komarzewski and Razumovsky; - a young castellan's son who came to St Petersburg via Riga with neither his father's leave nor a passport. He claimed to carry a letter from the Hetman to Potemkin. Deboli refuses to protect him, lends him 300 roubles against a bond and sends him home via Połock.

13 (27 July 1787). Foreign ministers await an audience with the Empress. She received three of them at Tsarskoye Selo, in a small circle and in very good humour. Hetman Branicki and his wife are to come to St Petersburg this winter (news from Cobenzl). There are hopes he will regain the King's favour. Deboli answers that the King does not push him away.

15 (31 August 1787). Three posts came with no letter. The answer to the King's letter will come from the Empress herself, since Ostermann's chancery has no orders. The British envoy (Fitzherbert) has left and was given the Empress's portrait. On Tuesday Ségur's tragedy "Coriolan" was staged at the Hermitage, with only Cobenzl and the author invited. Comedies and proverbs are played in the small theatre; the other ministers come on Thursdays. Ségur leaves within a week with the Prince de Ligne, after M. de Sainte-Croix's arrival. The letter is left unsigned as Deboli leaves for Pavlovsk.

21 (17 August 1787). Deboli asks how the King's letter and its allegorical idea were received. The Empress came back to town, without saying whether she would return to Tsarskoye Selo. A ceremony was held at the Summer Palace for the Preobrazhensky regiment's feast. She then moved into the Winter Palace, to everyone's satisfaction.

23 (14 September 1787). Courier to Warsaw; Cobenzl and the Austrian courier; the Turks have declared war; French mediation; Ostermann on France and Berlin; Sardinia; Prussian recruitment (2 × 500); the prince de Ligne wishes to write to the king.

28 (25 September 1787). Back from Gatchina; the king's letter of the 12th; Cobenzl says the alliance binds the Emperor to war; Council debate on peace with the Turks; Ligne's letter sent with the Austrian courier; Ligne asks about an extraordinary sejm; Deboli jokes he will propose him as deputy for Wilno.

30 (3 August 1787). Pisarz Wielhorski has arrived on business of the castellan's wife Ogińska of Wilno (probable), with the chancellor's letters to the vice-chancellor, Count Bezborodko and Prince Vyazemsky (probable); Deboli has introduced him. Starosta Potocki: 200,000 roubles would have been lost had they not been withdrawn, merchants having failed (partly unresolved); creditors will get barely 5 %. Potocki still loses through the exchange rate, down to 36 stuivers (probable) per rouble against 42 at the start of winter, on the 400,000 roubles he sent.

33 (7 October 1787). At tomorrow's conference Deboli will carry out the king's order (dispatch of the 24th of last month): Field Marshal Rumyantsev's division has hastened its entry into Turkish territory to screen Poland; he will ask when to expect the answer on the alliance project with Russia ("in hand"); there is hesitation here about starting anything in Poland and fear of trouble from Prussia; Deboli answers that inaction would be taken as abandoning Poland and would help Prussian intrigues. Three conclusions: 1) no long war is wanted: take Ochakov (this autumn or rather in winter), then make peace; 2) according to Bezborodko the Emperor will do little; Herbert has not yet sent a courier because Joseph II wants to be ready and to concert with Russia; the attack will come when the Russian army enters Ochakov Tartary and Moldavia, the Emperor also attacking from Pokutia if Kamieniec is secured; the theatre of war will move to the Danube; 3) a Franco-Russian union is hard: England would join Prussia; the Danish minister (Saint-Saphorin, probable) foretells an English fleet in the Baltic, but has a second plan: Russia will humour both England and France. Ségur is almost the only one to speak of the prince of Nassau with respect; ministers here mock him. 200,000 roubles in gold and silver sent under escort to Rumyantsev to pay for provisions in Poland. Rumour of a 5-million loan (probable) at the Berlin bank, spread on purpose by Berlin, and false.

37 (16 October 1787 (part in code 444)). Written in the morning before leaving for Gatchina; the courier announced in the king's letter of the 3rd has not arrived. With the vice-chancellor away, a long talk with Markov on the dispatch: he is heard kindly and told Russia still wants to shield Poland from any damage in this war and to come to an agreement; but on guaranteeing a territory for Poland (asked in the king's letter) Markov protests and gives a "dissertation": in the last Turkish war circumstances forced Russia into the partition; if Poland makes difficulties Russia might again have to consent to its loss; the aim should be keeping, not enlarging, the country; Russia cannot promise unconquered land; anything would rather come from conquests over the Turks; above all Polish possessions must be preserved; spreading the plan would be most harmful. Deboli answers in two parts: 1) troubles in Poland will be prevented if Russia joins in the means of keeping Poland under the watchword of union; the nation, used to fear, would read Russian inaction as abandonment, and individuals would scatter "like lost men who fall into snares while seeking help"; 2) the idea of gains from the Turks is no sine qua non; he asks that it not be misconstrued; the proposal, known to few, is to come through Stackelberg and stay secret, as the vice-chancellor urged. He must now treat the matter with the vice-chancellor on these lines; Markov repeats that the disposition to an agreement remains and calls the use of the Polish army against the Turks a way to occupy minds and turn them from harmful ties. The rest of the piece is in other tables (9933, 4000): not read.

G1 (13 February 1787). Gołuchowski has nothing to add on the Empress's journey beyond his report to the Department. He denies what was reported about Prince Repnin (a sum of roubles and a place in the suite): it is untrue. Buchholtz reportedly announced the coming entry of 10 Russian regiments, causing alarm in Warsaw; questioned by the Prussian minister in St Petersburg, Gołuchowski said what he knew and refrained from saying more, since the matter was not clear enough in the report of the Palatine of Ruthenia.

G3 (30 March 1787). On Sunday at court the foreign ministers (Danish, St-Saphorin; Portuguese, Horta?) pressed him about the 10 regiments said to be entering Poland; he answered he had nothing certain. The Danish minister then asked about Şahin Giray: Hamburg papers said he would be sent to Persia and later return to the Crimea, where the Empress is to go. Gołuchowski said he knew no more than the Hamburg papers and ended the conversation to avoid further questions.

G4 (18 May 1787). Charged (by Prince Stanisław Poniatowski's household) with finding out Grand Duke Paul's taste in saddle horses to be sent from Poland, Gołuchowski questioned the riding master who had been at Tsarskoye Selo. The horse must be: 1) very calm; 2) unafraid of firing, attacks, arms drill, soldiers' shouts and cannon — not even moving its head when the Grand Duke, as he does, rides up to the guns; 3) lively when needed and well schooled; 4) sound and strong-legged, since the Grand Duke rides his chosen horse every day: he sets off at a gallop to a fixed point, then walks, out twice a day, sometimes up to 40 versts. The Grand Duke complained he had no good horse to sit before his regiment's front without fear and wants a Polish horse for the May review (Old Style). Gołuchowski objects that horses sent on 15 May will only arrive on 26 June; and he doubts that one horse can have all these qualities (the rest of the reading is in reading/g4.md, in Polish).

  1. The key test failed at the threshold set. Criterion written before the measurement: 0.90 of words read for sense on the held-out despatch (8 August 1788) and on the whole. Result: 0.837 and 0.864. The verdict was not rewritten. Two deviations are declared (alignment without a band; a notation bug y → i fixed after a first display at 0.824). A new test on three despatches of 1786 whose clears are in AKP 269 is pre-registered, not yet run.
  2. Where the unresolved words come from. 1,281 words, mostly isolated syllables that do not construe: misread digits of the despatches (read once, on the images), values of 444 that do not fit in place, four groups whose value is torn or rubbed out in the key. They are left as the key gives them.
  3. Probable and restored words. A word is “probable” when one letter or one syllable of the group is uncertain (doubtful digit, plausible neighbouring group) or when a proper name is recognised without being sure (Saint-Saphorin, Smiła, Ogińska). Only four words are restored from the sense (piece 4). Blind shape plates answered by Brice Dudout (shapes only, no value shown) settled a few digits: plate Z3a (piece 1: 1544 → 1644, 810 → 840, 1654 → 1657), plate Z3G (G1, G4: 1707 → 1767, 1557 → 1657, 1736 → 1756). The answers of plate Z3c (piece 33) are not yet applied (one word at most).
  4. Blind reading, clears of the time not opened. The cabinet’s clears for 1786–1787 are in AGAD, Archiwum Królestwa Polskiego, sygn. 269. The reader did not open them, so that they can serve later as a test. From the index of that register, a clear of the same date exists for eight of the fourteen pieces (right-hand column of the count): for those the content was very probably already known at the time, and our reading is a blind reading, not a discovery. For pieces 13, 21, 28, 33, G1 and G3 no clear was found.
  5. Prior work (checked again on 9 November 2026). No edition of the despatches of 1786–1787: the Polish Academy’s Institute of History edition (Korespondencja polityczna Stanisława Augusta. Augustyn Deboli, Ewa Zielińska and Adam Danilczyk) stops at 1782. But Zofia Zielińska (“Listy Stanisława Augusta z podróży do Kaniowa (1787)”, Kwartalnik Historyczny 110/4, 2003) quotes from AKP 269 Deboli reports of 29 December 1786 and 5, 9 and 18 January 1787, that is pieces 1, 4 and 7: their content is partly known from the clears; Jerzy Łojek (Misja Debolego w Petersburgu w latach 1787–1792, 1962) uses the correspondence of 1787 without editing it (not read by us). In Daniel Bourdeau’s repository, target 416 was open before our deboli1787 folder (PR no. 293, 6 November 2026); see also the related target deboli1788 (older code of 1788).

Method, validation and credits

Method: (1) AGAD shelfmarks and inventory checked; the 56 despatches and 4 letters of the volume sorted by opening group: 22 pieces in code 444 (signal 2345), 19 in table 9933, 14 in table 3865, 3 in 12282, 3 in the code of 1789–1791, 3 mostly in clear; (2) key ZbPop 444 transcribed in full and frozen before any decoding; (3) pre-registered test on three despatches of 1788 (AGAD ZbPop 428), ciphers transcribed and hashed before their clears (ZbPop 417): failed at 0.90 (0.837 on the held-out piece), key confirmed as that of 1783–1788; (4) transcription of the fourteen pieces read, digit by digit on the images, decoding with 444 v3, reading for sense and count by script on each reading file (restored words excluded from the rate). The clears of the time in AKP 269 stay closed.

Credits. Documents and key: Archiwum Główne Akt Dawnych, Warsaw (Zbiór Popielów sygn. 3, 444, 428, 417), images consulted for research only, not reproduced. Catalogue (nos. 415–416) and folders deboli1788–1791: Daniel Bourdeau (cyphersolver). Sorting, transcription, key test and readings: Brice Dudout, with Claude (Anthropic), 5–6 November 2026; page published 9 November 2026.

Unsigned report to a Majesty on Gabriel Bethlen, [1624] — partial reading

Among Camerarius’s papers in Munich, between letters of Gabriel Bethlen, Prince of Transylvania, to the Emperor (Kassa, 29 May 1624), lies a German report without date or signature, addressed to “E. M.” (Your Majesty). It deals with Bethlen, the peace with the Emperor, money for 24,000 men and the Margrave’s army. A one-page passage is in cipher: two-digit numbers for letters, four-digit numbers for words. A secretary of the time already deciphered it: most groups carry their meaning written above. We rebuilt the key from those glosses, then read by sense four of the six runs he left unglossed. This is not a new decipherment of the text, and the reading is not validated: there is no part that could have been held out for a measurement.

Date undated; filed among pieces of 1624 (after a letter of Bethlen dated Kassa, 29 May 1624)
Place not stated
Writer not named
Recipient “E. M.” (Euer Majestät) — probably not the Emperor, whom the text names in the third person (“von dem Kayser erlangt”); Frederick V, King of Bohemia, is likely given the Palatine provenance of the collection, but nothing on the leaf names him. Halm’s catalogue (1874, p. 123) has “Schreiben an den Kaiser”: the text contradicts it.
Source Munich, Bayerische Staatsbibliothek, Clm 10403, no. 65 (Collectio Camerariana 53), fols. 192–193; digitised microfilm MDZ bsb00116451, views 411–413 (cipher on view 412 only)
Cipher mixed: a homophonic alphabet of two-digit numbers (a = 6, 9 or 15…), a word code of four-digit numbers (1410 = Herr, 1628 = Jenner…), doubled letters for short words (ZZ = mir, Gg = dass…). Neither the Casimir 1629 family (shifts −6 to +6 tried) nor the system of lead 2182

Keywords Bethlen · E. M. · der löbliche Herr · künfftigen Jenner · feind · auffs eüsserst verfolgen

Digitised manuscript (MDZ) ↗
Target majesty1624 in Daniel Bourdeau’s repository ↗

State of the reading. Partial reading, explained; key rebuilt from the contemporary glosses; read by sense, not validated. What was glossed at the time is not our contribution (archive decipherment, credited “contemporary”). Our contribution: the letter key as a table, the reading of four of the six runs left without a gloss, and the correction of the addressee. Rule applied: Daniel Bourdeau’s, 95% of words read for sense; on this site “read” = certain + probable, restored excluded. Of the 6 unglossed runs: 3 certain, 1 probable {x}, 0 restored, 2 unresolved ‹…›; runs read: 4 / 6; letters read: 15 / 18 = 83.3%. The threshold is not reached. No measurement was made: the cipher fills one page, almost all glossed, and no other piece of Clm 10403 shares the code.

Conventions: plain word = period gloss or certain reading; {x} = probable; [x] = restored from the sense; ‹…› = unresolved; “…” = passage not in cipher or not transcribed. Normalised text; the code groups and the clear text around the passage are not transcribed here.

Cipher passage (period glosses and our readings)

Nun kan E. M. ich mit grundt der Warheit berichten, dz der [löb]liche Herr mir absonderlich zu {botten} ‹e?› {nehmen}, der meldet auch zu schreiben zugelassen,

dieweil er, dass zu ‹?e?› {wünden} würde, do wolte er … den künfftigen Jenner mit hülff … und … er macht …,

des … als dan … feind … auffs eüsserst verfolgen helffen.

Values read from the glosses on the same leaf, run by run; 8, 36 and 45 rest on one occurrence each; 62 may be s (“solte” rather than “wolte”); 27, 32 and 65 occur once and have no value. Word groups read from the glosses: 1410 Herr · 2638 schreiben · 1628 Jenner · 1007 feind · 1853 macht · 1779 lassen · ZZ mir · Yy zu · Pp er · Gg dass · LL der · aa do · 11 zu · 71 dz.

Summary of the sense

The writer assures “E. M.”, “on the ground of truth”, that a “worthy lord” (der löbliche Herr) has allowed him to write, and that, if a certain thing comes about, this lord means next January (den künfftigen Jenner), with help, “to pursue the enemy to the utmost”.

The summary rests on the period glosses and on our reading; the clear text around the passage is not transcribed.

Limits

  1. No validation. No part was held out (the cipher fills one page, almost all glossed); no other piece of Clm 10403 shares the code (sweep of 6 November 2026; no. 6 has only a cipher signature, not examined); no printed text was found. The readings rest on the sense and on the glosses of the time.
  2. A single reader (an agent), on a digitised microfilm; no human palaeographic check. Several glosses are hard to read (groups 1492 “botten?”, 2999 “nehmen?”, and run 62.61.42.36.19.45, glossed perhaps “zu zeitigen”, which the key gives as “wünden”, or “sünden” if 62 = s: probable, meaning unclear).
  3. Addressee. Halm (1874) lists the piece as a letter to the Emperor. The text names the Emperor in the third person and addresses “E. M.”: so it is another Majesty. Frederick V is a hypothesis, not a reading.
  4. Prior work (re-checked 9 November 2026). The period decipherment on the leaf covers most groups: it is a prior solution, and we do not claim the glossed text. Halm 1874, p. 123: catalogue entry only. Szilágyi 1879 (Bethlen’s letters): nothing for May 1624. Not available as full text: Briefe und Akten NF, Acta Bohemica, Gindely, Hurmuzaki, Tadra (AÖG). Not on DECODE, no other target in Daniel Bourdeau’s repository; a web search on 9 November 2026 finds no edition or decipherment of Clm 10403 no. 65.

Method and credits

Method: (1) the 19 runs of two-digit numbers on view 412 (77 numbers, 34 distinct) transcribed by eye, each with its period gloss; (2) the letter key of Casimir 1629 (and Paweł 1624), with every shift from −6 to +6, tried on the glossed runs: at best 2 letters of 20, ruled out; (3) letter values set from the glosses, run by run, then the key frozen (SHA-256 c4bd9a4d…); (4) applied to the six unglossed runs, re-read at high magnification on 6 November 2026, and counted by Daniel’s rule. No statistical measurement, for want of a held-out text.

Credits. Document: Bayerische Staatsbibliothek, Clm 10403, no. 65 (MDZ digitisation, Public Domain Mark 1.0; no image reproduced here). Interlinear decipherment: a secretary of the time. Lead no. 2181, with the Halm reference and the MDZ links: Daniel Bourdeau (cyphersolver), who hosts the target majesty1624 (PR no. 295). Transcription, key and readings of the unglossed runs: Brice Dudout, with Claude agents (Anthropic), 5–6 November 2026.

Lord Cobham to Walsingham, Ostend, April–May 1588 — key checked, four codes, R8490 read at 81% (partial reading)

In the spring of 1588, weeks before the Armada, Elizabeth I sent five commissioners to negotiate peace with the Duke of Parma’s deputies at Bourbourg. One of them, William Brooke, Lord Cobham, wrote to Walsingham from Ostend in clear English, with short passages in Greek-like signs and numbers. This target is Daniel Bourdeau’s (catalogue no. 131): he rebuilt the alphabet from the sibling letters glossed at the time and read in part the letter of 5 May (R8490). Our contribution is narrower: an independent check of the key on a held-out page, and four codes named by a contemporary gloss, which give their subject to two sentences of R8490. In a second pass we re-read all the cipher of R8490 with these codes: 81% of the cipher words read, hence a partial reading.

Dates R8489: Ostend, 16 April 1588 (fols. 78r–78v); R8490: Ostend, 5 May 1588 (fols. 80r–81)
Place Ostend → London
Sender William Brooke, 10th Lord Cobham, commissioner of Elizabeth I
Recipient Sir Francis Walsingham, Secretary of State
Source London, British Library, Harley MS 287; records DECODE R8489 and DECODE R8490 (images not reproduced)
Cipher simple substitution with homophones in Greek-like and arbitrary signs, two shared signs (Λ = s/t, γ = r/y), nulls, and a few codes (numbers and ◻) for people; the same system as the March–April letters, glossed between the lines at the time

Daniel Bourdeau’s target ↗
Our contribution (PR #343) ↗

State of the reading. Partial reading, explained; key checked. Rule applied: Daniel Bourdeau’s (95% of words read for sense; here “read” = certain + probable, restored excluded). R8490 is read in part: all the cipher of fols. 80r–80v (43 words and 6 codes) was transcribed and hashed before decoding, then decoded with the frozen fol. 78r key and a declared derived key (new values with their attestations, not measured). Read: 35 of 43 cipher words = 81% (21 certain, 14 probable; restored excluded: 0%); 8 unresolved; with the 6 glossed codes: 41/49 = 84%. Below the 95% threshold: partial reading. The clear text is Daniel’s transcription, checked only on the lines that carry cipher; no figure is given for the whole letter. R8489 carries its contemporary decipherment (interlinear gloss, “Decrypted” on DECODE): nothing is claimed on its text. What we publish: (1) the key, learnt on page f. 78r only and measured once on every glossed word of f. 78v (349 letters): 0.917 of letters right against at best 0.284 for 200 shuffled keys (criterion fixed in advance: 0.85 and best + 0.30) → validated; (2) the codes 22, 26, 27 and ◻.

The cipher passages of R8490 (Daniel Bourdeau’s clear text, cipher re-read, codes applied)

… to drawe our forces from ‹…›, hoping theym {in} the [◻ : the States] ‹…ances›, for what chaunces so ever yow bestowe … yt will not be {kept}, the haven is ‹…› (f. 80r, ll. 9–12)

Touching hostages, yt ys honorable for [7 : the Queen] to ‹…› ther surti to these {termes}, as usuall yn all {treats} … at the {treat} of {Breda} … and the subiect ther were delivered Julio Romeo, Cristophero Mondragon, Mor Daussy … (f. 80r, ll. 18–21)

[22 : Sir James Croft] is so {forwarde} yn the {action} that he promised Q[ueen] to send to {Bruges} [27 : Dr Dale] to begyn the openning of the ‹bookes?›, which myght bee to the ‹…› of ‹…›, that a {brother} about [15 : the Duke of Parma], who promised the mayor ‹…› a {haven} to open (f. 80r, ll. 31–35)

Clear text: Daniel Bourdeau’s transcription (texts/R8490_reading.md in his target). Cipher words in italics, in the cipher’s spelling; {x} = probable; ‹…› = unresolved; codes in bold brackets (22, 27, ◻ identified by us; 7 and 15 already in Daniel’s target). New compared with his reading: Bruges (unread there), kept, Breda letter by letter, subiect singular, termes; the small closed o (= d) is told apart from ∞, and d is o throughout. Still unresolved: where the forces are drawn from (l. 9), “…ances” (l. 10), the state of the haven (l. 12), the verb of l. 19, two words of l. 33 and the mayor of ‹…› (l. 34). Word-by-word table: dudout/reading_R8490.md in the PR. Sense: Croft, one of the five commissioners, pursued his own contacts with Parma and was imprisoned on his return; Dale and Rogers were the commission’s two civil lawyers.

Limits and prior work

  1. Declared deviation. The fol. 78v crops used to transcribe the held-out cipher also showed the glosses (they sit just above the cipher lines). The key was already frozen; the risk is a bias in reading a few ambiguous signs. Word agreement: 0.684 (not decisive); every error comes from the shared signs (Λ, γ) and from “d” = o, absent from fol. 78r.
  2. Not done. The 8 unresolved words of R8490; the derived key was not measured against a control; the target’s letters R8492, R8495, R8496 remain unread.
  3. Prior work, re-checked on 9 November 2026. The target and the alphabet are Daniel Bourdeau’s; codes 7, 10, 15 and 16 were already glossed there, 22 and 27 were open. R8489 is deciphered at the time. No printed decipherment is known (the Calendar of State Papers, Foreign 21/4 does not calendar these Harley letters, per Daniel’s notes).

The French ambassador at Rome, 10 August 1547: a cipher copy and its decipherment of the time — partial reading

In a gathering of August 1547 in the chancery of Cosimo I at Florence, a few weeks before the murder of Pier Luigi Farnese, there are three intercepted cipher copies. Daniel Bourdeau spotted them (lead no. 2339) around a letter of Cardinal Alessandro Farnese (c. 78r) that remains unread. Next to it, c. 76r copies in figures “a chapter of a letter from Rome of 10 August 1547”, and c. 79r carries, under the same heading, its decipherment of the time: the French ambassador reports that he advised the young Henri II to keep what his father had left him rather than seek glory in a war. The text is therefore known from c. 79r: this is not a new reading. Our contribution is the key to this cipher, rebuilt on the pair and measured on held-out lines, where it is only partial.

Date Rome, 10 August 1547 (“Copia d’un Cap.lo d’una l(ette)ra di Roma de x d’Agosto 1547”); copy made in the Florentine chancery
Place Rome → [the French court]; intercepted copy → Florence
Sender the French ambassador at Rome (not named in the text)
Recipient [Henri II], from the text; the copy is a “chapter” quoted in another letter
Source Florence, Archivio di Stato, Mediceo del Principato 384, c. 76r (cipher) and c. 79r (decipherment of the time); images on ASF PAD, unit 969 (not reproduced)
Cipher homophonic substitution with a prefix code: 6, 8 and 9 alone stand for e, o, a; every other code has two digits (01 = r, 05 = n, 23 = t, 70 = i…), a few stand for a syllable or a word (10 = che, 24 = et); a dot over a digit does not change the value; nomenclature codes for names (Ambasciatore, Francia, Inghilterra) remain unknown

Digitised manuscript (ASF PAD) ↗
Our target in Daniel Bourdeau’s repository (PR #344) ↗

State of the reading. Partial reading, explained; key partial by our protocol; text already known from its decipherment of the time (c. 79r). Rule applied: Daniel Bourdeau’s, 95% of words read for sense; here “read” = certain + probable, restored excluded. By the key alone, of the 243 words: 131 certain (53.9%), 61 probable {x}, 51 restored [x] from c. 79r, 0 unresolved; words read: 192 / 243 = 79.0% (100% with the restored ones). The threshold is not reached. State of the key: learnt on lines 1 to 13 of c. 76r only, measured once on the held-out lines 14 to 18: 0.695 of letters right against at best 0.218 for 200 shuffled keys; 0.85 was needed to call it validated (criterion fixed in advance): it is partial. Cardinal Farnese’s letter (c. 78r) is not read.

The words are those of c. 79r, spelling of the copy, without accents or punctuation; where the cipher says something else, see “Limits”.

Count (words)

code6890103040507101214151720212324274047505152537074

A value is kept if the code is seen at least twice on lines 1 to 13 and gives that letter in at least 20% of cases. 34 gives “tm” (uncertain). Rare codes and the nomenclature are missing: they account for the 51 restored words and the only partial measurement.

Summary of the sense

The French ambassador at Rome wrote to his King some days ago, in a short discourse, that the greatest glory he could win at the start of his reign was to look to his guard, keep what his father had left him and govern himself well; that the desire to gain by breaking into war went against him, given the great dangers; that he was young and would have time for better occasions.

The writer understands that the ambassador was given to know that, with the King’s ardour for some enterprise, hoped for by great men of France, he could not be held back; that those over there who tried to turn him from it were thought men of little spirit; and the ambassador was urged to do all he could to stay united with England and win it over entirely. The last sentence is the hardest; its sense remains uncertain.

Limits, prior work and credits

  1. The text is not new. c. 79r is the decipherment of the time of c. 76r (same heading). We claim no reading and no solution: only the key, as a reusable table, and its measurement.
  2. The cipher sometimes says something else than the decipherment. c. 79r retouches the wording: “al suo Re mostrandoli che…” (79r: “al suo Re, che…”); “romper guerra o entrare in qualche impresa”; “mostre da chi” (79r read “da Dio”); “per una passione” (79r read “passata”, probably our misreading of 79r); “portava altrimenti” (79r “dissuadeva”); “ritenerlo o ritirarlo” (79r “et”). The cipher is the source.
  3. Restorations. The 51 restored words fall on codes absent from the key: mostly the opening (“L’Amb.re di Francia”, probably nomenclature codes), Ambasciatore (3 times), Francia, Inghilterra, più, sperandosi, and rare homophones. No restoration contradicts a letter given by the key.
  4. Transcription. A single pass, by an agent, on the 2000 px image, with no independent re-reading; slips in the figures are likely (dots, 1 and 7, 0 and 6).
  5. The Cardinal’s letter (c. 78r) is not read. The tables of A. Meister, Die Geheimschrift im Dienste der päpstlichen Kurie (1906), pp. 176–177, nos. 1 and 2 (coded by Daniel Bourdeau), and the Klee key fail on it (0.174, 0.183 and 0.098 by a criterion fixed in advance). The c. 76r key, only partial, was not applied to it, as our protocol required.
  6. Prior work, re-checked on 9 November 2026. No target for this gathering in Daniel Bourdeau’s repository before ours; his review of 6 November (Della Casa–Farnese correspondence, ed. Comelli 2022, vol. II, in full text; DECODE; Cryptiana; Lasry) found no edition or study. The content remains that of the decipherment of the time.

Method: protocol written and hashed before either page was transcribed; the cipher transcribed without looking at c. 79r, then the clear, both hashed before any alignment; lines 14 to 18 held out, never aligned or deciphered before the measurement; key taken from the alignment of lines 1 to 13 only and frozen; a single measurement (character agreement, 200 controls with permuted values); then the whole page deciphered and compared word by word with c. 79r.

Credits. Lead and review of the gathering: Daniel Bourdeau (catalogue no. 2339, cyphersolver). Decipherment of the time: Florentine chancery, c. 79r. Images: Archivio di Stato di Firenze (not reproduced). Key, measurement and reading: Brice Dudout, with Claude (Anthropic), 9 November 2026 (PR #344).

Walsingham to Wotton, 10 September 1585: the sign words — partial reading

In the summer of 1585 Elizabeth I sent Edward Wotton as ambassador to the young James VI of Scotland. Walsingham’s letters are in clear, with a two-digit name code, but the one of 10 September (DECODE R4844) also hides some twenty words in a sign alphabet, whose interlinear decipherment was struck out on purpose. These letters are Daniel Bourdeau’s targets (walsingham1585, wotton1585): he identified most of the name code and judged these words “too short, no key”. Our contribution: the same alphabet is deciphered at the time in five other letters of the volume; a key taken from three of them and measured on a fourth is partial, but it reads 16 of the 19 groups of R4844 and corrects one name code.

Date the Court, 10 September 1585
Route London → Scotland
Sender Sir Francis Walsingham, Secretary of State
Recipient Edward Wotton, ambassador in Scotland
Source London, British Library, Add MS 32657, fols. 194–195 (DECODE R4844); pairs deciphered at the time DECODE R4689, DECODE R4835, DECODE R4836, DECODE R4837, DECODE R4845 (images not reproduced)
Cipher two systems: a two-digit name code and a sign alphabet with homophones (÷ = r or s; ω = e, h or g), squares and triangles as null markers

Daniel Bourdeau’s target ↗
Our contribution (PR #345) ↗

State of the reading. Partial reading, explained; key partial by our protocol. Rule applied: Daniel Bourdeau’s (95% of words read for sense; here “read” = certain + probable, restored excluded). Of the 19 sign groups of R4844: 11 certain, 5 probable (including “[a]bsent”, one letter restored), 3 unresolved: 16 / 19 groups read; in letters, about 84% without the restored ones (86% with). The threshold is not reached. State of the key: learnt on R4689, R4835 and R4836 only; one measurement on R4845, transcribed blind by one agent and glossed by another (29 words, 178 letters): 0.646 of letters right against at best 0.213 for 200 shuffled keys; 0.85 was needed to call it validated: it is partial. Additions made after the measurement are untested.

Grades: S = certain, P = probable ({x}), R = restored letter ([x]), I = unresolved (‹…›). The struck-out interlinear decipherment of the time is not used.

Summary of the sense

The plot set down by the Master of Gray (39) is to be judged; the banished lords (28, 29) and 30, “of best judgment”…; Her Majesty (3) will not make herself a party; Walsingham wants no “violent course” in these great disorders; Wotton is to be absent at the attempt, keep his train at Stirling and avoid suspicion. Postscript: a letter from the Lord [Scrope?] touching the secret plot, which was not carried with the secrecy wanted.

Correction: Daniel read 3 as “France” (grade M) from a Wotton draft; the pairs gloss it three times as the Queen or England. 10 (the King), 19 (Arran), 36 (England), 39 (the Master of Gray) and 40 (the Justice Clerk) are confirmed.

Limits and prior work

  1. Partial key. The errors come mostly from homophones not yet separated. One transcriber per part (agents), no human palaeographic check.
  2. Prior work, re-checked on 9 November 2026. Targets and name code: Daniel Bourdeau (R4840 to R4843 read, R4844 “decoded, not read”). DECODE marks the pairs “Decrypted” and R4838–R4844 “Non-decrypted”. No edition of the R4844 sign words is known (the Calendar of State Papers, Scotland viii does not calendar the letter of 10 September, per Daniel); Read, Mr Secretary Walsingham, and the CSP Foreign 1584–1585 are not re-checked here.

Carsten Anker to Prince Christian Frederik, London, 28 June 1814 — Princess Charlotte (read)

In June 1814 Norway had just given itself a constitution and a king, the Danish prince Christian Frederik, but Sweden, backed by the powers, claimed it. In London his confidant Carsten Anker sought England’s support. On 28 June he slipped into his mail a small leaf, partly in cipher: the match of Princess Charlotte of Wales, heiress to the British throne, with the Prince of Orange had just been broken off, and Anker brought back his “old idea”: to marry Christian Frederik to the princess. The leaf had never been deciphered: it has no clear of the time and is not in the printed edition of the correspondence.

Date London, 28 June 1814 (“fr. 28 Junii 1814”)
Place London → Christiania
Sender Carsten Anker, Christian Frederik’s envoy in London
Recipient Prince Christian Frederik, regent then King of Norway (May–October 1814)
Source Oslo, Arkivverket / Riksarkivet, RA-EA-5938 Christian Frederik, F/Fc/L0217/0002, PDF p. 59 (“ad Anker C. 101a”), on Arkivportalen (images not reproduced: no explicit reuse licence)
Cipher homophonic substitution in symbols (a = + / ✕ / ȣ; e = ⊘ / Z; o = ⊙ / ⊍) with a few logograms (# = jeg), mixed with clear Danish and French; the alphabet of Anker’s letter of 31 December 1811

Our PR to Daniel Bourdeau (#347) ↗

State of the reading. Read (98.8%). Daniel Bourdeau’s rule: 95% read for sense; here “read” = certain + probable, restored excluded. 252 cipher signs: 249 certain or probable (98.8%); restored: one logogram (3 occurrences, 1.2%) read [D.K.H.] = “Deres Kongelige Høihed” (Your Royal Highness), from “D. K. H.s” in the clear; one word, ‹felv›, decoded but of uncertain sense. Key: learnt on p. 9 only of the 1811 cipher letter, with its glosses and its clear of the time, then frozen; measured once on a held-out part (p. 10, left column): 0.950 of letters right against at best 0.019 for 200 shuffled keys → validated. A first measurement, with a pencil key card from the same archive, had failed (0.025): it is declared. Before decoding, the leaf was compared with the archive’s alphabets: 0.937 of its signs have a value in the 1811 key, against 0.369 for the Bergen 1814 alphabet.

The leaf (Danish of 1814)

Parti{e}s med Pr: af {O}ranien er afbr{u}dt pour jamais. N{u} opstaaer min gamle Idée : Prindcesen er sm{u}k, har en megen fast Care{k}ter, skal absol{u}t giftes. — {U}d af Landet faaer h{u}n ikke Lov at gaae, og det maatte man finde sig i. — Var nu [D.K.H.] ei b{u}nden og oplystedes Norriges Horizont saa var Idéen vel værd at overtænke. — Grunden og selve Bygningen til N. stadige Lykke, Roe og Velstand var da med et lagt og mesten færdig. Om 8 à 14 Dage bliver [D.K.H.]s Portrait færdigt, godt st{u}kket og p{u}bliceret. Men dette er en vidtløftig Materie, som kræver Tid. K{u}n at [D.K.H.] ei binder sig! Gud veed, at ingen kan ivrigere end jeg ønske D. K. H.s sande Lyksalighed. Min hulde ædle og elskede Herre! At De høre deem ikke ‹felv› til. Hardenberg og jeg have meget talt herom og vi ere eenige.

Decoded cipher in bold, the manuscript’s clear in italics; {x} = probable (new shape, value fixed by several words); [x] = restored; ‹…› = unresolved. The princess is not named on the leaf: she is Charlotte of Wales, from the break with the Prince of Orange (June 1814).

Translation

The match with the Prince of Orange is broken off for ever. Now my old idea comes up again: the Princess is handsome, has a very firm character, and must absolutely be married. — She will not be allowed to leave the country, and one would have to put up with that. — If now [Your Royal Highness] were not bound, and Norway’s horizon brightened, the idea would be well worth weighing. — The foundation, and the very building, of Norway’s lasting happiness, peace and prosperity would then be laid at a stroke and nearly finished. Within 8 to 14 days [Your Royal Highness]’s portrait will be finished, well engraved and published. But this is a large matter that needs time. Only let [Your Royal Highness] not bind yourself! God knows that no one can wish more ardently than I for Your Royal Highness’s true happiness. My gracious, noble and beloved Lord! That you do not belong to them ‹felv›. Hardenberg and I have talked about this a great deal, and we are agreed.

Prior work and limits

  1. Prior work, re-checked on 9 November 2026. The leaf is deciphered neither in the archive nor in C. J. Anker’s edition (Christian Frederik og Carsten Anker’s Brevveksling 1814, Royal Danish Library, Danmarks Breve; full-text search of 254 letters), which does print the 1811 cipher letter (no. 32) and the code dispatch of the same day (no. 88). Nothing in Daniel Bourdeau’s repository.
  2. The marriage project itself is known. Christian Frederik writes of “the intended connection with Princess Charlotte” in his printed letters to Anker of 24 June, 11 October and 12 December 1814 (nos. 31, 39, 43). The leaf adds Anker’s own proposal, on 28 June, in cipher. No historian’s study of the project was found in a quick search.
  3. Limits. One transcription, by an AI agent, by shapes but not blind (the Danish words read through simple signs); no second reader. The held-out part had been read before in print no. 32: the shuffled keys (0.019) show the score does not depend on it.

Credits. Manuscripts, glosses and 1811 clear of the time: Arkivverket / Riksarkivet (Oslo), RA-EA-5938, via Arkivportalen. Edition and context: C. J. Anker (ed.), Royal Danish Library, Danmarks Breve (public domain). Key, measurement and reading: Brice Dudout, with Claude (Anthropic), 9 November 2026 (PR #347 to Daniel Bourdeau).

The Florentines at the court of Louis XII, 20 October [1514] — an ambassador for Rome and the Este towns (partial reading)

In the autumn of 1514 Louis XII had just made peace with England and married Mary Tudor. The Florentine chancery of Francesco Pandolfini, Florence’s orator at the French court, copied for Rome “two chapters” of a letter of 20 October, in clear broken by three cipher passages. The lead is Daniel Bourdeau’s (catalogue no. 2389): he found six cipher letters without decipherment in the filza, beside cipher/decipherment pairs of the time in the same system. We rebuilt the key from those pairs and read in part the first of the bare letters.

Date 20 October [1514] (“pace et parentado fatto”: the Anglo-French peace and the King’s marriage, 9 October 1514)
Place French court → Rome (copy)
Sender the Florentines at Louis XII’s court (chancery of Francesco Pandolfini)
Recipient Rome (copy of “ij cap.li scripti ad Roma”)
Source Florence, Archivio di Stato di Firenze, Mediceo avanti il Principato LXXII, no. 322, c. 401r (images not reproduced)
Cipher cipher consonants carrying the vowel as a superscript (1 to 5 = u, o, i, e, a), homophones, word signs (F = et, M = non, T = senza) and a nomenclator between points (.2. Pope, .4. Most Christian King, .64. Holiness)

Daniel Bourdeau’s lead (no. 2389) ↗
Our PR ↗

State of the reading. Partial reading, explained; key partial. Daniel Bourdeau’s rule: 95% of words read for sense; here “read” = certain + probable, restored excluded. About 168 cipher words, about 77% read (none restored: 0%): block 1 about 74 words (41 certain, 27 probable, 6 unresolved, about 92%); block 2 about 24 words (9, 4, 11, about 54%); block 3 about 70 words (30, 18, 22, about 69%). These counts are approximate: the cipher does not mark word boundaries. Key: learnt on the filza’s pairs of the time (345/346, 340/341), frozen, then measured three times on held-out parts: 0.788 and 0.691 (under the 0.85 threshold: not validated), then, with an Italian n-gram criterion calibrated in advance, N = 0.613 → partial, under a lenient “partial” threshold, declared. A few values (.3. Emperor, .64. Holiness…) were added after the measurement in a derived key, declared and not measured.

The cipher passages (Italian)

1. Et ‹.51.› {ti} ha {detto} che arrivato Rocciafort {qui} subito si {manderà} costì uno homo per {ambasciadore} di questa Maestà, il quale noi {crediamo} che sarà il {vescovo} di {Lancres}, con {havere} {chiarito} avanti il {suo} partire di qui {questa} Maestà ‹…› potere negotiare il {tutto} ‹…› {Santità}, con il {quale} ‹.51.› crede che {invero} ‹…› {habbia} a venire la medesima differentia che al presente {è} {tra} sua {Santità} et {monsignore} di {Marsilia}.

3. Et di più {richiese} questa Maestà che volessi parlare dello {oratore} {Vinitiano} ‹…› che quella {Signoria} {relassassi} ‹…› che ‹…› {dice} che al presente ‹…› {della} {sua} ; et ‹…› {ce} ne ha dato {la} notitia ; non si ricordava ‹…› {pensiamo} che {possino} et {Monselice}, {Este} et {Montagnana}, delle quali ‹…› {ci} ricorda {crediamo} ‹…› che ‹…› investiti {dello} {imperadore}.

{x} = probable; ‹…› = unresolved; unmarked = certain. Block 2 (two lines) is too full of gaps to quote: “{ti} harà facto {significare} la {commissione} che porta ‹…›”.

Translation and sense

Block 1. ‹.51.›, an informant at the French court (code unresolved), has {told} {us} that once Rocciafort arrives the King will at once send to Rome a man as {ambassador}, who we {believe} will be the {bishop} of “{Lancres}” (see not identified), empowered before he leaves to negotiate {everything} with His {Holiness}; ‹.51.› believes the same quarrel will arise as the one now between His {Holiness} and the bishop of {Marseille}. Block 3. After Alfonso Ariosti’s visit for the Duke of Ferrara, the King asked that the {Venetian} {ambassador} be approached so that the {Signoria} {give up} […] {Monselice}, {Este} and {Montagnana}, towns of the Padovano held by Venice which the Este hold as fiefs from the {Emperor}.

Prior work and limits

  1. Prior work, re-checked on 9 November 2026. No decipherment of the time for 322 (Daniel Bourdeau’s check of the untitled clear copies on 6 November; neighbouring pieces checked). Desjardins and Canestrini, Négociations diplomatiques de la France avec la Toscane, vol. II (1861), have a gap from 16 August 1514 to 25 May 1515. Lead 2389 is open; nothing else in Daniel’s repository. The text is therefore new, as far as we know.
  2. Limits. One transcription, by an AI agent, from images of middling resolution: superscripts often sit one sign off and δ/d are confused (declared defects, tolerated in the reading for sense). Code .51. and several marks (T with an n or x above, L with a c above) are not in the key.
  3. To come. The lead’s other bare letters (307, 309, 310, 311, 333) are being read.

Credits. Lead, finding of the bare letters and the pairs: Daniel Bourdeau (catalogue no. 2389, cyphersolver). Manuscripts and decipherments of the time: Archivio di Stato di Firenze, Mediceo avanti il Principato LXXII (images not reproduced). Key, measurements and reading: Brice Dudout, with Claude (Anthropic), 9 November 2026 (PR).

The Saxe-Altenburg envoys at the Westphalian congress, 1647–1649 — the key recovered and an unread postscript (read)

During the negotiations for the Peace of Westphalia, the envoys of the small duchy of Saxe-Altenburg at Osnabrück, Wolfgang Conrad von Thumbshirn and August Carpzov, wrote to the councillor Johann Friedrich von Brand. Their letters of 1647 hide a few sentences in numbers, each with its decipherment of the time. A later postscript, however, had never been deciphered: a single sentence in cipher, a lament.

Dates letters of 13 November to 25 December 1647; postscript fol. 399, undated (late 1648 or early 1649)
Place Osnabrück → Altenburg
Senders Wolfgang Conrad von Thumbshirn and August Carpzov, envoys of Saxe-Altenburg
Recipient Johann Friedrich von Brand, councillor of Duke Frederick William II
Source Landesarchiv Thüringen – Staatsarchiv Altenburg, Schönbergische Sammlung, Nr. 85; ThULB record and images (CC BY 3.0)
Ciphers two systems: in 1647 a homophonic substitution in numbers (2 or 3 numbers per letter, 5 to 90), whose key is missing from the file; and Thumbshirn’s signed key (image 0003), a simple substitution of 24 letters in numbers 1 to 52, written “in a continuous series” so that words cannot be guessed

Our PR to Daniel Bourdeau (#349) ↗

State of the reading. Read. Daniel Bourdeau’s rule: 95% of words read for sense; here “read” = certain + probable, restored excluded. Postscript 0837: 23 words of 23 read (100%): 20 certain, 3 probable (two numbers under a stain), 0 restored (0%), 0 unresolved; read with Thumbshirn’s key as it stands, 112 numbers, none outside the key. The 1647 letters: their text is known from the decipherments of the time (nothing new); our contribution is the homophonic key, rebuilt from the slips of 13 and 17 November and 22 and 25 December, then measured once on the held-out letter of 24 December: 0.966 of letters right against at best 0.245 for 200 shuffled keys → validated. Declared deviation: the reading of the postscript rests on the period key and the sense, not on this measurement, which tested the other system.

The postscript (fol. 399)

O miseros {nos} servos. Gott weis und hat meine {Zehr[e]n} {geseh[e]n}, die ich bereit viel vergos[s]en üb[e]r der schandlich[e]n Servitut, darein wier geführet.

Spelling of the cipher; {x} = probable; [x] = letter left out by the encipherer, added. Before the cipher sentence, the clear text speaks of “mein Patron”.

“O wretched servants that we are! God knows, and has seen the tears I have already shed so often over the shameful servitude into which we have been led.”

Prior work and limits

  1. Prior work, re-checked on 9 November 2026. Nothing in Daniel Bourdeau’s repository. No edition of the letters of Nr. 85: the ThULB record cites none; the Acta Pacis Westphalicae, Meiern (1734–1736) and M.-E. Brunert’s study of Saxe-Altenburg at the congress (based on Nr. 86) do not print them. All the 1647 cipher has its decipherment of the time; the postscript has none: it is the only new text.
  2. Limits. One transcription, by an AI agent. The measurement validates the 1647 key, not the reading of the postscript (another key, of the time, used unchanged). A possible link with the Magdeburg envoys at Osnabrück (Bourdeau catalogue no. 1639) was not examined.

Credits. Images and manuscripts: Landesarchiv Thüringen – Staatsarchiv Altenburg, Schönbergische Sammlung, Nr. 85; digitisation ThULB Jena (urn:nbn:de:urmel-stat-251122), licence CC BY 3.0. Key, measurement and reading: Brice Dudout, with Claude (Anthropic), 9 November 2026 (PR #349 to Daniel Bourdeau).
